articles.title: Washington blasts DOJ over noncitizen voter findings, claims 'glaring deficiencies'
articles.summary: Washington is pushing back on DOJ's noncitizen voter findings, saying its review found U.S. citizens, inactive voters and other "glaring deficiencies" in the federal list.
articles.body: Washington's secretary of state blasted the Justice Department Wednesday after federal officials said investigators had identified more than 400 noncitizens illegally registered to vote in the state, some of whom they said had cast ballots in multiple elections dating back decades.Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs pushed back against the findings, saying the state’s review of the list uncovered "several glaring deficiencies." "This list includes United States citizens and is not reliable. Without individualized proof of ineligibility, it would be both irresponsible and illegal for election officials to decline to process a registered voter’s ballot," he said. "That analysis reflects a significant number of people on your list who are not currently registered to vote or are on inactive status, contradicting your representations that all the individuals included in the list will receive a ballot in this year’s election," he added. On Monday, the U.S. attorneys’ offices for the Eastern and Western districts of Washington said investigators had identified lawful permanent residents, or green card holders, who were registered to vote or had cast ballots. "We have identified over 400 noncitizens who are registered to vote and have voted in multiple elections. This is only the tip of the iceberg," Neil Floyd, acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, said in a statement. "We will continue to investigate and identify those who are committing crimes by voting illegally." Immigration officials told Fox News Digital Tuesday that dozens of noncitizens have also been arrested nationwide in a major voter fraud crackdown. DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS In an interview with Fox News Digital, Floyd said investigators identified hundreds of noncitizen voters by reviewing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) records, which showed that some people who applied for certain benefits had also voted. While some individuals voted only once or three times in past elections, Floyd said others voted as many as 27 times. In total, his office counted approximately 1,500 instances of noncitizens casting ballots. He emphasized that some noncitizens had been voting for decades, predating Washington’s transition to a vote-by-mail system. "I think the earliest moment we have is 1984," Floyd said. "It's early ‘90s, late ’80s, I believe." However, Floyd said he had not checked whether any of the individuals voted in the upcoming midterms, explaining that he did not want to "interfere with the current election." The number of potential noncitizen voters could represent only a fraction of the broader population, Floyd said, because the list includes only individuals who sought certain benefits in Washington state. NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS "If you take that population, and you expand it out to include all the people that are here illegally that we haven't had contact with, just my estimation is that it's going to be in the thousands," Floyd said. Federal officials said many green card holders were registered to vote without their knowledge through Washington’s Motor Voter program, which integrates voter registration into the state’s Department of Licensing. "We have heard from green card holders who were registered against their knowledge via the Washington Motor Voter program. Then they receive a ballot in the mail and assume they are legally registered — that simply is not the case," the notice said. According to the Washington secretary of state’s website, eligible residents are automatically registered to vote only if they provide proof of U.S. citizenship during a driver’s license or ID card registration process. Floyd said investigators identified patterns they believe contributed to noncitizens being registered to vote. According to the DOJ notice, federal officials are asking Washington state to set aside ballots cast by the identified individuals until their citizenship status can otherwise be confirmed. "Washington is now on notice that noncitizens are voting. It is up to the state to take action to make sure that they are not allowing these noncitizens to vote illegally," the notice said. The move builds on DOJ's legal action against California, where federal officials are seeking to set aside mail-in ballots from roughly 20,000 voters they allege are likely noncitizens while their citizenship status is verified. In response, the California secretary of state’s office said last week that its review "found significant accuracy problems with their sweeping claims.""At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt. At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election. Plaintiff’s sole claim—that a federal criminal prohibition on individual noncitizen voting preempts large swaths of California’s election administration—borders on the absurd. The relief Plaintiff seeks is as unlawful as it is untenable," the statement said. Officials warned that voting as a noncitizen can have serious consequences for those seeking to become U.S. citizens. Potential criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application, and some individuals could also face charges for fraudulent voter registration. On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security told Fox News Digital numerous illegal aliens had also admitted to unlawfully registering to vote or casting ballots in U.S. elections. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of the dozens of suspects arrested, at least 18 had voted in a federal election. The individuals were from a range of countries, including Mexico, Somalia, Honduras, Guyana, Cuba, Germany, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Vietnam, El Salvador, Cambodia, Guatemala, Portugal and Italy. Many also faced charges for numerous alleged crimes, including counterfeiting, fraud, kidnapping, DUI, sexual offenses, assault with a dangerous weapon, drug possession and burglary.

articles.title: How the Cheesecake Factory got dragged into a spat involving Trump and Obama days before the midterms
articles.summary: The former president compared the White House renovations to a Cheesecake Factory operated by Saddam Hussein, prompting a pointed response from the commander...
articles.body:
With a week to go until the 2026 midterm elections , you'd be forgiven for thinking that President Trump and former President Barack Obama were running against each other this year.

While campaigning for Democrats in Ohio over the weekend, Obama mocked the various renovation projects that Trump has been overseeing at the White House, prompting a pointed response from the president and his administration.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations," Obama told the crowd in Cleveland. "He should be on HGTV. Guy's building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House. He's paved over the Rose Garden. He's put a helicopter pad on the South Lawn. And there's gold everywhere — what's up with the gold? Everything, more gold. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Obama also skewered the Trump administration for the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool controversy.

"Remember that whole thing about 'drain the swamp'?" he said. "The only thing that got drained was the reflecting pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up, and then they tried to blame a three-time Olympian and say he vandalized it."

Obama also taunted Trump for starting a trade war with "that well-known evil empire, Canada."

"I mean, these are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short," Obama said.

But it was the Cheesecake Factory line that seemed to strike a nerve with Trump .

In a Truth Social post hours after Obama spoke, Trump called Obama a " grossly incompetent President " but did not address the Cheesecake Factory comment. On Monday, the White House account on X posted a digitally altered image of the restaurant's menu listing what it described as Trump's accomplishments, saying, "The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments."

Then on Tuesday, the White House hosted an hourslong YouTube livestream titled "Lo-fi Beats to Dismantle DEI To," featuring a split-screen of what the administration described as Trump's efforts to dismantle DEI and an AI-generated cartoon of the president waving to a crowd of Americans in front of a Cheesecake Factory.

At a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday, President Trump praised the restaurant chain as "a very successful company," which is true: The Cheesecake Factory was opened by David Overton in California in the 1970s to showcase his mother's cheesecakes. The company now owns and operates 383 restaurants throughout the United States and Canada. (The company did not respond immediately to Yahoo's request for comment.)

Trump then defended the need for White House renovations — which are projected to cost at least $900 million — while denying that he has spent too much time focusing on them.

"The White House represents our country, and that has to be pristine," Trump said in Corinth, Miss., while stumping for incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. "I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand. He doesn't understand the White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful. It can't have cracks in the column."

Trump insisted that he had spent "very little time" on redesigning the White House, but also said that he has "fun doing it" and that "it actually relaxes me."

"I do it very good," he said. "I'm really good in real estate and fixing things. I fix things very good, very beautifully and I always build beautiful and inexpensive, which is a good combination if you can do."

Most Americans, though, disapprove of the president devoting his time to such projects. An ABC News/Washington Post poll conducted earlier this month found 59% of U.S. adults say Trump is spending "too much" time on renovating the White House, compared with 27% who say he is spending the right amount of time and 11% who say not enough.

The president, whose overall approval ratings are near all-time lows, has been out on the campaign trail hoping to help Republicans avert a so-called blue wave and hold on to control of Congress.

In recent stump speeches, Trump has urged would-be voters to pretend he's running to encourage a bigger turnout.

"In this election, if you would, I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," he said in Mississippi.

Obama has been out on the trail too. He's seeking to boost Democrats in key races, such as those in Ohio and Michigan, as the party looks to flip both chambers of Congress.

But Trump suggested Obama is campaigning against him.

"He fought me with crooked Hillary [Clinton]. That didn't work out well. Then he fought me with Kamala [Harris]. That didn't work out well," the president said. "And now they say, 'Oh, whoa. Barack Obama is going to start campaigning.' And he's not even campaigning. Tell him he's not campaigning about me. Maybe he'll go home."

articles.title: Conservative influencer James O’Keefe charged with unlawful voting and identity theft in Minnesota
articles.summary: O’Keefe was charged alongside fellow influencer Cam Higby. They are accused of misrepresenting themselves at polling places during Minnesota’s primary in August.
articles.body: A Minnesota prosecutor charged conservative provocateur James O’Keefe and influencer Cam Higby on Wednesday with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft after they showed up at polling places in August using the names of registered voters. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who announced the charges at a news conference, accused the pair of entering polling places during state primary election voting on Aug. 11 and identifying themselves using the names of registered voters in those precincts without those voters’ knowledge or permission. “Both men stopped short of signing the oath we all sign before receiving our ballot,” she said. “But Minnesota law states clearly that no individual shall intentionally misrepresent their identity in applying for a ballot.” O’Keefe and Higby were using a process under Minnesota law known as vouching. It allows people to vouch for other voters on Election Day. A registered voter who lives in the same precinct can vouch for up to eight voters, while staff members of residential facilities can vouch for their residents. The pair of influencers disguised and recorded themselves going undercover using hidden cameras at the polling places. They posted videos capturing their interactions on social media in August. O’Keefe said on X that they dressed in “Muslim garb” — including, for one of them, a full-face veil known as a niqab — and that their goal was to “expose the sheer lunacy of Minnesota’s ‘vouching’ system.” Moriarty said Wednesday the office of Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon alerted her office to their conduct. After O’Keefe and Higby’s videos became public in August, Simon said in a statement that their “apparent goal was to cast doubt on one or more Minnesota election laws that have been in force for over fifty years. Instead, they revealed their ignorance of how those laws actually work — while putting themselves in legal jeopardy.” “The misconduct by this group is outrageous and totally unacceptable,” Simon added. “We have zero tolerance for lying, lawbreaking, and disruptions at our polling places.” Police interviewed the registered voters whose names O’Keefe and Higby used, said Moriarty, who added that they also used the names of deceased voters. Asked where they obtained those names, Moriarty said, “We don’t know that.” Moriarty said that they are not in jail and that instead, they will be issued summonses to appear in court in Minnesota. Neither O’Keefe nor Higby immediately responded to requests for comment. President Donald Trump has alleged for years that Democrats have committed voter fraud or have rigged elections against him. As part of those efforts to crack down on and prevent purported voter fraud, the Trump administration has been targeting Democratic-controlled states by trying to obtain state voter roll lists and identifying alleged noncitizen voters. O’Keefe has been involved in other voter fraud-related incidents. In 2024, he and Project Veritas, which he founded, settled a lawsuit brought by a Pennsylvania postmaster after the group promoted a postal worker’s false claims of voter fraud during the 2020 presidential election. O’Keefe was removed as the head of Project Veritas in 2023. Higby was a journalist for conservative outlets and now operates a YouTube account with 285,000 subscribers.

articles.title: El-Sayed accused Biden of exploiting 9/11 mastermind's killing in resurfaced attack: 'Troubling'
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed accused Joe Biden of exploiting the Ayman al-Zawahiri drone strike to bolster his party's approval before the midterm elections.
articles.body: When American forces killed one of the architects of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed criticized then-President Joe Biden, accusing him of using the operation to boost his political standing rather than focusing on the significance of the strike. On Aug. 1, 2022, Biden announced that Ayman al-Zawahiri had been killed in a U.S. drone strike. "He was deeply involved in the planning of 9/11, one of the most responsible for the attacks that murdered 2,977 people on American soil," the president told the nation following the strike. Intelligence officials have long held that al-Zawahiri was involved in the planning behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks as well as other deadly assaults on Americans overseas. CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS El-Sayed condemned al-Zawahiri as a terrorist in an essay, but criticized Biden for what he portrayed as an attempt to capitalize politically on the strike. "President Biden is using the strike to bolster his approval here at home. It is troubling to watch yet another American president flog ‘War on Terror’ themes to resurrect a laggard term," El-Sayed wrote in 2022 for The New Republic. "This strike, then, offers the Biden administration a fig leaf, demonstrating that even in Taliban hands, Afghanistan is not off-limits for direct action against terrorist targets." EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY El-Sayed argued that Biden was using the killing of al-Zawahiri to bolster his political standing ahead of the looming midterm elections He went on to argue that, if Biden was serious about "projecting strength in the Middle East," he would challenge some of the autocratic leaders in the region with whom the United States had traditionally aligned. While El-Sayed criticized Biden's handling of the death of al-Zawahiri, he condemned the al-Qaeda leader in no uncertain terms, calling him a "craven terrorist" who "died with the blood of innocent civilians on his hands." The Washington Free Beacon was the first to report on the newly unearthed essay. ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS El-Sayed has previously criticized other high-profile U.S. military and counterterrorism operations. Similarly, when President Donald Trump ordered the 2020 drone strike of Iranian military leader Qassem Soleimani, El-Sayed warned that "one shouldn't kick a rabid dog." When President Barack Obama’s administration killed terrorist Anwar al-Awlaki, a U.S. citizen living in Yemen, El-Sayed characterized it as an "extrajudicial assassination." El-Sayed has also compared Trump to Osama bin Laden, suggesting that both inspired people to engage in terrorism and that Trump should be held to account like bin Laden was. Bin Laden was killed by American operators in May 2011. articles.title: Indiana senator stepping down if reelected after shoplifting allegations
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Indiana state Senator Ron Alting is stepping down after allegations of shoplifting at several Walmarts across Indiana and Florida. Alti...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Indiana state Senator Ron Alting is stepping down after allegations of shoplifting at several Walmarts across Indiana and Florida.

Alting shared in a social media post that his recent actions are the product of possible cognitive decline, and he is working with medical professionals to diagnose and resolve the issue.

"After many difficult conversations with my family, my doctors and people I have trusted for many years, I have concluded that I need to bring my time in public office to an end and devote my attention to my health and my family," he said.

Alting, a Republican, has served the 22nd Senate district for 28 years, since his first election in 1998.

With the General Election on Tuesday, Alting's decision could have an impact on voters, as Alting's name remains on the ballot.

He has arranged with the state senate president that in the case of his reelection, the Republican Party will select his replacement through their vacancy protocol.

"Under Indiana law, a vacancy in the state legislature is filled through a caucus of eligible precinct committeemen from the district representing the same political party," the Indiana Republican Party told The Center Square in a statement. "The caucus is generally required to select a replacement within 30 days of the vacancy occurring."

"I have great confidence that this process will produce an outstanding leader who will serve Senate District 22 and its people well," Alting said.

The Indiana Democratic Party responded to the news with a statement from Chair Karen Tallian.

"This story speaks for itself. It is a sad and disappointing tale," Tallian said. "Fortunately, there is a candidate who offers a bright, fresh alternative. Natasha Baker is a well-respected high school teacher who is engaged in the community and will do a great job."

Baker shared concerns that a vacancy replacement marginalizes voters in the decision.

"Sen. Alting's announcement that he intends to resign if reelected raises important questions about who would ultimately represent our district and how that decision would be made," Baker said. "Voters deserve a senator elected by the people, not hand selected by party insiders."

The Republican Party has not released possible names for replacement.

Elkhart County Prosecuting Attorney Vicki Elaine Becker is investigating the shoplifting allegations.

articles.title: DOJ fires back at Dem AG over Election Day guidance telling officials when to call cops on federal agents
articles.summary: The Justice Department slammed Jay Jones' Election Day guidance as "bluster" after Virginia advised poll workers to call police on DOJ monitors.
articles.body: The Justice Department blasted Virginia Democratic Attorney General Jay Jones' Election Day guidance as "bluster and political posturing," pushing back against his 10-page directive advising local election officials to call police when federal agents approach polling places and to document their activities. The Oct. 15 bulletin, jointly issued by Jones' office and the Virginia Department of Elections, outlines how officials should respond to federal agents, scrutinize requests from DOJ election monitors and prepare for potential federal demands for ballots and voting equipment. The dispute comes as conservative litigation firm America First Legal pursues records concerning the state's warnings about potential federal election interference, which Fox News Digital has learned. "The Virginia Attorney General's performative actions attack a strawman," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "DOJ's election monitors will be engaging in the same routine monitoring we've done for decades." SPANBERGER AG DRAWS FIRE OVER TWO-FRONT FIGHT AGAINST TRUMP ENFORCEMENT AGENDA "We're hopeful local election officials in Virginia continue their longstanding practice of allowing DOJ election monitors into polling places to evaluate for compliance with federal law," the spokesperson continued. "The Virginia AG's statement reads as nothing more than bluster and political posturing for his own self-interested purposes." DOJ has already announced it plans to send election monitors to Democratic-heavy Fairfax and Prince William Counties. Del. Wren Williams, R-Stuart, an attorney who battled Jones over Democrats’ failed redistricting-related litigation, said Jones has his election-security priorities backward. "Jay Jones wants poll workers collecting ICE agents’ badge numbers, but God forbid they verify a voter’s ID," Williams said. "Plus, I thought Democrats said illegals weren’t voting, so who exactly is Jones trying to protect?" MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY Virginia still requires voters to present identification or sign an identity confirmation statement, although legislation enacted this year eliminated Election Day challenges to individual voters' qualifications at polling places. The blueprint noted that ELECT — the Virginia elections agency — received multiple inquiries about how to respond to federal representatives showing up at polls. It instructed election officials to consult with lawyers and establish communications with local prosecutors and police: "Having these discussions prior to Election Day ensures that election officials can provide their perspective to local law enforcement about what counts as intimidation and interference during elections, including issues related to the presence of unauthorized individuals." "If, for example, an armed individual attempts to gain access to a polling location, officials should call local law enforcement immediately," it added in a section addressing unauthorized individuals and prohibited conduct. The bulletin separately advises officials to consider contacting police and counsel if federal agents approach or enter polls, while cautioning against physically obstructing them. Virginia State Sen. Danny Diggs, R-Poquoson — the former sheriff of York County — told Fox News Digital that in his 45 years in law enforcement he never saw an officer or official observer "make a polling place less safe." "I routinely visited every polling place, inside and outside, while armed and in uniform and was always welcomed by election officials and voters. The Attorney General apparently thinks otherwise," Diggs said. He also called it "reckless" for the attorney general's game plan to urge election officials to confront federal observers. On Page 4, the plan says ordinary DOJ monitors must obtain local authorization to enter polling locations, under rules similar to those for neutral observers. If a DOJ monitor requests access, the plan prescribes that local registrars discuss the scope of the monitoring with the agency before consenting, and "consider asking whether DOJ is assessing compliance with civil or criminal federal laws." The bulletin also advises election officials to consult attorneys and prepare to respond to federal subpoenas seeking ballots or voting equipment. Fox News Digital reached out to Jones and ELECT for comment and a response to critics. Jones, however, spoke out days earlier after launching a related new Voter Protection Section within his office. "I was raised by people who understood that the right to vote was never simply given. Generations of Americans had to sacrifice, organize, and show extraordinary courage to claim that right," Jones said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. "That history is personal to me, and it reminds us that the work of civil rights and voting rights is never finished. "That is why we created a dedicated Voter Protection Section within the Office of the Attorney General. This work now has a permanent home, and a team focused every day on defending voting rights and enforcing Virginia law. Virginia votes every year, and protecting the franchise must be a year-round responsibility. In Virginia, the right to vote will be defended." Virginia Beach attorney Tim Anderson also analyzed Jones' gameplan, calling it a "remarkable directive to election officials." "While all this is happening, Virginia has eliminated the ability to challenge a voter's qualifications at the polling place," Anderson said. "Think about what we're witnessing: The attorney general is preparing election officials to scrutinize federal law enforcement while Virginia has eliminated a longstanding Election Day safeguard for questioning voter eligibility," he said in a statement. "The bulletin identifies no specific planned unlawful federal operation in Virginia." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER America First Legal (AFL) exclusively told Fox News Digital on Tuesday it filed a public-records request Monday seeking legal analyses and communications behind the bulletin, records concerning Jones' newly launched Voter Protection Section and inquiries about federal election monitoring. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The dispute now turns on what evidence, if any, prompted Jones' office to prepare for potential federal interference at Virginia polling places, and whether the records sought by America First Legal will shed light on the attorney general's concerns ahead of Election Day.

articles.title: New poll shows Ramaswamy's ad of Acton's mother didn't win over voters
articles.summary: A new Ohio poll finds Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Acton changed few minds and may have hurt him instead.
articles.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy 's ad featuring Democratic rival Amy Acton's estranged mother didn't win over voters, according to a new Suffolk University-USA TODAY Ohio poll.

If anything, the ad may have made voters view Ramaswamy less favorably, said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center.

Ramaswamy, who is backed by President Donald Trump , launched an ad Oct. 22 featuring Acton's estranged mother accusing her daughter of lying about her past and her political opponent. Acton hasn't spoken to her mother, Donna Arthur, since 1978, when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with rape for sexually abusing a young Acton. The Arthurs left Ohio before Cledith Arthur could face trial.

Obama joins Amy Acton and Sherrod Brown for Cleveland rally — Photos

Nearly three-quarters of those polled, 72%, had seen or heard about the ad within days of its release. But it changed few minds. Seven respondents said the ad caused them to switch from Ramaswamy to Acton. Only one respondent said the ad caused them to switch from Acton to Ramaswamy.

"You only do an ad like that if you're trailing by a large margin," Paleologos said of Ramaswamy's "Hail Mary strategy." "You have to take a gamble, and sometimes the gamble pays off, and you score, and sometimes the pass gets intercepted or blocked."

New poll shows Acton, Ramaswamy locked in a tight race

In the new poll conducted after the ad ran, the Ohio governor's race was too close to call. Acton had a slight edge over Ramaswamy, 48% to 44%, while Libertarian candidate Don Kissick received 3.6%. The poll of 500 likely voters was conducted Oct. 21-26 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points.

The poll also surveyed 300 additional likely voters in Portage County, a longtime political bellwether east of Akron, which Trump won by more than 15 percentage points in 2024. Of those polled, 47.3% backed Acton, 46.7% supported Ramaswamy and Kissick pulled 2%. The margin of error for that subset was plus or minus 5.6 percentage points.

Paleologos said pollsters captured Ramaswamy's support better in the October poll than in their September one, where Acton led Ramaswamy, 50.4%-41.4% . This time, pollsters conducted callback sessions with people who initially said they were undecided or refused to answer. But ultimately, "Ramaswamy still isn't anywhere near where he needs to be," Paleologos said.

Did the ad hurt Ramaswamy more than Acton?

The poll indicates the ad likely hurt Ramaswamy's image more than Acton's. According to the new results, 54.2% had an unfavorable view of Ramaswamy, up from 52.2% in last month's poll. About 41% had an unfavorable view of Acton, which was the same as last month's poll.

Brenda Malcolm, of Columbus' Northland neighborhood, said she still hasn't decided who she'll pick for Ohio governor, but the ad made her lean toward Acton.

"It just totally ticked me off," said Malcolm, who described herself as an independent voter. "To go contact a mother that hasn't seen her daughter in 50 years and get this statement from her. The mother doesn't know anything about Amy."

But Leah Kelm, 35, who lives in Northeast Ohio, said she would choose anyone over Acton, the state's former health director during the initial months of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"I'm not 100% sure I think he's running a super effective campaign," Kelm said of Ramaswamy. "I just remember Amy Acton doing her wine with DeWine during COVID and feeling a little lied to with the whole COVID response."

Those polled were much more likely to say Ramaswamy was running a negative campaign, 49.8% of respondents, than Acton, 15.2%. Another 11.6% of respondents said both candidates were to blame for the negativity in the governor's race.

Could Libertarian Kissick be the 'kiss of death' for Ramaswamy?

Brandon Freeman, 45, of Toledo, isn't voting for Acton or Ramaswamy after criticizing them for "throwing dirt on each other's names." He instead backed Libertarian candidate Kissick, saying government should be less involved in people's lives.

"They pay all this money for all of this advertising going into their campaign, and it's 90% slander," Freeman said of Ramaswamy and Acton. "Just boost yourself. Tell people what you're going to do that's really going to make a change and difference and stop focusing on the other candidates."

If enough Ohioans vote like Freeman, Ramaswamy could be in trouble, Paleologos said. Among independents polled, Kissick got 7% of the vote, compared to 58% for Acton and 25% for Ramaswamy.

"(Kissick) is a ballot option for people who are conservatives, who will never vote Democratic but are just not excited about Ramaswamy, either because of the ad or because they just don't like him," Paleologos said.

If Kissick pulls a few percentage points from Ramaswamy, Acton wouldn't have to win the majority of the gubernatorial vote, Paleologos said.

"The 50% rule is out the window if Kissick gets 3%," he said. "Kissick could be the kiss of death for Ramaswamy."

Reporters Haley BeMiller and Emma Wozniak contributed to this article.

State government reporter Jessie Balmert can be reached at jbalmert@usatodayco.com or @jbalmert on X .

articles.title: Appellate court rules in favor of Abbott days before election
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - Texas' highest appellate court has ruled in favor of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in a lawsuit brought by his Democratic challenger over...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) - Texas' highest appellate court has ruled in favor of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in a lawsuit brought by his Democratic challenger over access to public records days before the Nov. 3 election.

State Rep. Gina Hinojosa sued the governor earlier this month, requesting that a Travis County district court require him to provide details for a public information request she submitted in late September. Under Texas Government Code, a government body is required to provide information to a member of the state Legislature, including confidential information, if the public information request states the information is needed for legislative purposes. The Legislature does not convene until next January.

Hinojosa was seeking access to communications exchanged between the governor and trillionaire Elon Musk, who has donated millions of dollars to Republican campaigns in Texas. Musk is listed as the top donor to Abbott's campaign, with contributions totaling $5.5 million, according to transparencyusa.org .

The communications "bear directly on many matters within the legislature's responsibility, including state incentives, state grants, broadband deployment, public health access, environmental impact, AI and data center development," the lawsuit argues.

During the COVID-19 lockdown era, Musk relocated much of his business operations to Texas from California. The trillionaire has since expanded them and established headquartered in Texas including for SpaceX, Starlink, Tesla, X, the Boring Company, Neuralink and xAI.

Hinojosa argues that Musk and his companies are receiving political favors in exchange for campaign donations. Her campaign has largely alleged that Abbott "does the bidding of his billionaire donors while leaving Texans to fend for themselves."

Billionaire Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker donated $1.2 million to Hinojosa's campaign, making the Democratic governor the biggest contributor.

Abbott's campaign has prioritized meeting with everyday Texans, including in their homes across the state. His platform includes plans to lower energy and housing costs, continued job creation and expansion and reduced costs for students, The Center Square reported . The state has also awarded contracts and grants to a range of billion- and trillion- dollar companies to expand operations in Texas, The Center Square reported.

In response to the public information request, the governor's office provided 1,374 pages, the majority of which were redacted, according to Hinojosa's lawsuit. She then requested un-redacted documents, which the governor's office didn't provide. She sued to gain access to them, saying Abbott "refuses to comply with his clear legal duty" and is "breaking the law" by not providing them, her lawsuit alleges.

District Judge Catherine Mauzy ruled in her favor and ordered the governor's office to provide the unredacted documents, saying Hinojosa "has an immediate legal right to access the requested documents."

Mauzy did not recuse herself from the case after having donated $500 to Hinojosa's campaign in June, Bloomberg News first reported. In 2016, she contributed more than $700 to Hinjosa's first campaign for the Texas House, Bloomberg reported, citing campaign finance records.

According to the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure , judges must recuse themselves from any proceeding where their "impartiality might reasonably be questioned." And the Texas Code of Judicial Conduct says judges "should act at all times in a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary" and not "advance their private interests" among other prohibitions.

Mauzy, who is running for reelection, didn't respond to requests for comment.

After her ruling, the governor's office filed a petition with the 15th Court of Appeals to intervene, which it did. It issued a stay on the lower court ruling and gave Hinojosa two weeks to respond to Abbott's interlocutory appeal.

The new appellate court hears cases related to the state government. All three of its inaugural justices are running for reelection, The Center Square reported.

Abbott's campaign has argued that Hinojosa could have requested the documents more than a year ago when the Legislature was in session but chose to do so roughly one month before Election Day and sued when early voting was underway.

"Hinojosa's desperate attempt to use her official office to benefit her own campaign is just the tip of the iceberg. She's conspiring with the unethical judge who ruled in her favor," his campaign said.

On the same day as the appellate court ruling, Hinojosa said in a social media post , "Elon Musk just gave Greg Abbott $5 million. Sounds like the Elon emails Abbott has been hiding must be more damning than we even knew."

After the ruling, Abbott's Press Secretary Andrew Mahaleris issued a statement saying, "This was a sham lawsuit in a rigged district court. The trial court judge refused to follow the law and rubber-stamped an illegal fishing expedition into the Governor's Office. The appeals court rightly froze this abuse of process."

Throughout the litigation process, Mahaleris commented on social media that Hinojosa was "abusing her official capacity as an outgoing lawmaker for political purposes."

Early voting is ongoing through Friday. Abbott has a slight lead in a race that according to some polls is statistically tied, The Center Square reported.

articles.title: Peltola campaign's alleged Dan Sullivan spoiler plot takes new turn as DOJ faces major legal hurdle
articles.summary: The Department of Justice's Alaska Senate race lawsuit faces hurdles as legal scholars debate whether anonymous ballot analysis can prove confusion.
articles.body: The Department of Justice faces an uphill legal battle in Alaska, where it is trying to convince a federal court that confusion between two Senate candidates with nearly identical names could be enough to delay certification of the election results. Roughly two weeks before Election Day on Oct. 22, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking to delay certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses and votes cast for another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could have changed the result, pending an investigation into whether voters mistakenly selected the wrong candidate. The DOJ's complaint stems from a controversy in Alaska where two individuals by the name of Dan Sullivan, one a retired schoolteacher and the other the state’s incumbent senator, appear alongside each other on the state’s ballots. Although Alaska has traditionally been a Republican stronghold in Senate elections, the state's race could carry greater national significance this year as Republicans seek to defend their narrow Senate majority. The New York Times reported Wednesday that the campaign of Mary Peltola, the Democrat running for Senate in Alaska, reportedly worked with operatives to recruit another Dan Sullivan to run for Alaska’s Senate seat, hoping voter confusion would draw support from the incumbent Republican senator. Citing interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit, the Times reported that the effort also targeted other potential spoiler candidates, despite the Peltola campaign’s repeated denials of involvement in the second Sullivan’s candidacy. TODD BLANCHE CHALLENGES DANA BASH FOR ONLY CITING PART OF CONSTITUTION DURING HEATED ELECTION CLASH Fox News learned Wednesday that federal prosecutors are conducting an "aggressive criminal investigation" into how the second Sullivan secured a spot on Alaska's ballot, according to two sources familiar with the probe. Investigators are preparing grand jury subpoenas and examining potential violations of voters' rights, with the investigation expected to continue beyond Election Day. The DOJ declined to comment. On Sunday, Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee filed a proposed motion to dismiss the Justice Department's lawsuit, arguing that the federal law cited by the DOJ governs voter registration, not candidate eligibility or ballot design. They also urged the court to resolve the case before Election Day. Conservatives have argued that two similar names on the same ballot could possibly lead to voters who would prefer to reelect the state’s Republican senator accidentally voting for the retired school teacher. Opponents of the effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot argue that sharing a name with an incumbent is not grounds for disqualification and that Alaska's ranked-choice voting system allows voters to rank both candidates, potentially limiting the effects of mistaken selections. Alaska’s Division of Elections initially sided with conservatives, disqualifying Sullivan the schoolteacher by finding that his candidacy was not a genuine, good-faith bid for office but instead was designed to confuse voters into mistaking him for the senator. Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews overturned the decision in June, holding that the Division of Elections had no authority to void a candidacy on that basis. Alaska's general election ballot identifies the incumbent as "Sullivan, Dan S.," with Republican and incumbent designations, while listing the other candidate as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," without a party affiliation, a measure some argue is enough to clear up potential confusion. Lawyers at the Justice Department, however, remain unconvinced. Although Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested that officials could examine ranked-choice ballot patterns for signs of confusion, the Justice Department has not explained how those patterns could establish that individual voters mistakenly selected the wrong candidate. Voter privacy protections pose a major obstacle to a potential federal case, as it would be nigh impossible to tie specific voters to specific ballots to serve as evidence of confusion. ALASKA HAS A VOTING SYSTEM LIKE NO OTHER STATE; REPUBLICANS WORRY IT COULD COST THEM IN NOVEMBER "This is just the stuff that is just impossible to measure after the fact," Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller said of the DOJ’s plan to infer voter intentions from anonymous ballots. Blanche, in interviews with the press, has provided some insight into how he would like the DOJ to go about solving this problem. "So, because of rank-based voting, voters… they write not just one, not just two, but multiple names on the ballot. And so there are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates," Blanche told CNN’s Dana Bash. Blanche's comments suggest that the Justice Department could examine ranked-choice ballot patterns for potential signs of confusion, although such patterns alone would not establish whether voters intended to support a different candidate. "It will be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused, and that could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot," he said in a later interview with CBS. ALASKA REPUBLICANS SCRAMBLE TO EDUCATE VOTERS ON SUSPECTED DEM PLANT AS 'BALLOT FATIGUE' THREATENS RACE Don Palmer, senior legal fellow for election integrity at the right-of-center Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital that he feels the Justice Department might have a case if the agency's lawyers construct it properly. Statistical analysis of ballots alone, he maintains, will likely not be sufficient to convince a judge of the administration's position. "You'll have the opportunity to interview witnesses, do some statistical analysis, and make a decision whether or not the campaign wants to contest the results of the election," Palmer said. "So it's actually quite a high standard where you have to bring in witnesses. You can't generally just prove it with some statistical analysis… the campaign would have to show to the court through statistical and expert testimony, plus witness testimony, plus affidavits, that enough voters were confused, that they made inaccurate choices on what they intended to do. Then and only then could the court determine whether the race should be overturned." "If voters voted for the non-Republican Dan Sullivan as their first choice, but voted down ballot for Republicans as their first choice otherwise, that could indicate patterns of confusion whereby voters were looking to vote straight Republican as their first choice and were prevented from doing so because the inclusion of Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot confused matters," a spokesman for the America First Policy Institute told Fox News Digital. Ben Hovland, a senior fellow at the left-of-center Center for American Progress and an expert on elections, was more bearish on the DOJ’s prospects. SEEING DOUBLE: SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES, SETTING UP BIZARRE ALASKA SENATE BALLOT "You've never seen a claim like this made under the National Voter Registration Act," he told Fox News Digital. "This is not a matter of federal law. This is a state ballot qualification issue and the Alaska Supreme Court addressed this issue months ago. For the Department of Justice to step in at this point and sort of make this claim, you know, doesn't appear to be about winning in a lawsuit because it doesn't seem like there's any scenario where [they win], this is clearly about trying to sow confusion or sow doubt or set the stage to undermine the results of the election if the administration doesn't like what the voters will have to say." Walter Olson, a senior legal fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, also isn't convinced that the Justice Department will be able to get its case off the ground. "I wouldn't expect Blanche's local allies to get very far in this effort unless a federal court rules in favor of his theory that Alaska violated federal (as opposed to state) law by letting the schoolteacher stay on the ballot," Olson told Fox News Digital. "I think the state is likely to beat Blanche in federal court on that point, and that should end the case." Alaska has already moved to have the DOJ's case dismissed. articles.title: 'Radical Left Lunatic' judge Trump wanted impeached takes up Ilhan Omar warrant fight
articles.summary: Judge James Boasberg, a frequent Trump legal foe, now oversees the fight to unseal the FBI search warrant used in the raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home.
articles.body: A federal judge who has become a frequent legal thorn in the side of President Donald Trump and his allies is now presiding over a fight to unseal the warrant used to search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. The battle over whether to unseal the search warrant comes amid two separate federal investigations into the Democratic congresswoman stemming from concerns about discrepancies between financial disclosures filed a year apart and allegations that her father committed fraud when completing immigration paperwork. Omar immigrated to the United States from Somalia in 1995, when she was 12 years old. Investigators are examining whether her father misstated her age on his citizenship paperwork in 2000, potentially allowing her to obtain citizenship through him as a minor. Trump, a longtime foe of the progressive congresswoman, has been vocal in his attacks against Omar, having also accused her of committing immigration fraud by allegedly marrying her brother — referring to her first husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. In the weeks following the Oct. 12 raid on Omar's Washington, D.C., home, Trump called for Omar to be "put in jail." TRUMP SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD GO TO JAIL OR BE DEPORTED, CALLS HER ‘A DISGRACE TO OUR COUNTRY’ But the fight over whether to unseal the records is being overseen by Chief Judge James Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, an Obama appointee and longtime target of Trump. In March 2025, after Boasberg temporarily blocked deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members, Trump called him a "Radical Left Lunatic of a Judge, a troublemaker and agitator" and called for his impeachment. Trump also accused Boasberg of bias, saying it was "virtually impossible for me to get an Honest Ruling in D.C." The raid on Omar’s home came just weeks before the midterm elections, as alleged fraud in Minnesota’s social services programs had become a major political issue in the state. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS Days after Department of Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI conducted a raid on Omar's home under a search warrant issued by U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, three separate requests were made to unseal the warrant — by the New York Times; Judicial Watch, a conservative watchdog group; and 14 press organizations. Boasberg ordered the Justice Department to defend its position on keeping the warrant sealed in response to a consolidated request from the Times and 14 press organizations by Oct. 22, but he extended the deadline following a Justice Department request to wait until the search warrant was "fully executed." The Justice Department argued that releasing the information could compromise the integrity of the investigation. "This request sounds rash because it is rash," Pirro wrote. "The Court should reject it without prejudice for renewal after the search warrant has been fully executed and a charging decision is made public." The filing indicated that the Justice Department was still in the process of executing the search warrant, while other details about the investigation and warrant records remained redacted from the public record. But the Times and other media groups argue that the physical search occurred weeks ago and that any sensitive information in the warrant should be redacted rather than the entire warrant being withheld. Meanwhile, Omar is engaged in a separate dispute with the Justice Department. Her attorneys have demanded the return of property seized from her home, arguing that agents violated protections for her congressional work. They have also alleged that agents failed to provide her with a copy of the warrant and prevented her from contacting her attorneys during the search. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE Boasberg’s oversight of efforts to unseal the records follows a series of decisions that have drawn criticism from Trump and his allies. In June 2025, he ordered federal agencies to preserve Signal messages exchanged by senior officials while discussing U.S. military strikes in Yemen, saying the communications could constitute federal records. During the Biden administration's Arctic Frost investigation, he signed nondisclosure orders barring phone carriers from notifying Republican lawmakers that prosecutors had subpoenaed their records. Boasberg also drew criticism over his sentencing of former FBI attorney Kevin Clinesmith. Clinesmith pleaded guilty to altering an email used in an application to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to renew surveillance of Carter Page, a former Trump campaign adviser suspected of acting as a Russian agent. Boasberg, who previously served a seven-year term on the FISA Court, said Clinesmith’s alteration of the email undermined the court’s integrity but was a misguided mistake that provided Clinesmith no personal benefit. He sentenced Clinesmith to 12 months of probation and 400 hours of community service. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Boasberg said in his sentencing decision that he believed Clinesmith's role at the center of a years-long media "hurricane" had provided sufficient punishment.

articles.title: Dueling rallies thrust deep-red Lone Star town into the center of the political universe
articles.summary: Dueling rallies in Lubbock put the Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico on full display as Trump joined the Republican side.
articles.body: LUBBOCK, Texas — Two rallies, two crowds and two very different visions for Texas converged in deep-red Lubbock on Tuesday night as Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico made their cases to voters. Trump supporters camped out at Lubbock’s Civic Center as early as Monday night, calling the event a "once-in-a-lifetime experience." About four miles away, roughly 4,000 Talarico supporters descended on the neighborhood around the Fiesta Center. The rallies put Lubbock’s political identity on display. Long a ruby-red Republican stronghold, the city is now a battleground in a Senate race in which polls show Talarico narrowly leading Paxton. Outside Paxton’s rally, supporters remained confident the Lone Star State would stay red. 'Everything we can to keep Texas, Texas' Jenny, who traveled from Brownsville, dismissed the idea that the race was close. "What else do the Democrats have? They have Talarico going against Paxton," she told Fox News Digital. "All they’ve got is the ability to try and make people think that it’s close and there is no point in voting." "No, it’s not close," Jenny added. "Paxton is going to wipe the floor with him." MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD Eric, a Lubbock resident, also predicted a Republican win, saying Democratic policies do not align with his views. "Most of the Democrats that you talk to, when you start talking common sense to them, a lot of them, they don’t know if it’s a red or a blue policy, and a lot of them line up with red as well," he said. "It’s gonna stay red, absolutely." Nathan, from Milton, said he wants to preserve what he sees as Texas’ traditional values, including gun rights and opposition to abortion. "I want to make sure we are keeping all the normal values that we have in Texas," he said. "I want to make sure that we are keeping our guns, we are keeping our safety, keeping abortion as far away from Texas and do everything we can to keep Texas, Texas." 'This is the year that we flip blue' Across town, Talarico supporters said Trump’s appearance alongside Paxton showed Republicans were worried about losing ground in a reliably red state. "Trump’s in Lubbock? Trump’s in Lubbock, Texas? He’s scared, he is scared," one supporter told Fox News Digital. Natalie, from Friona, also viewed the same-day rallies as a sign of nervousness. "I think they have to be nervous, and I think it’s performative, like to come the exact same day as he is here," she said. "I really hope so, and looking at all of this, I think it is." DEEP IN TRUMP COUNTRY, A NEW GENERATION REVEALS THE DIVIDE BEHIND TEXAS’ TIGHT SENATE RACE Elias, a Lubbock resident, said Paxton’s reliance on Trump reflected poorly on the Republican candidate. He pointed to Paxton’s past controversies and impeachment by the Texas House. "I think it shows that Paxton is a weak leader," Elias said. "He had a chance to kind of redeem himself despite his ugly past, but he’s not a man, he can’t stand up for himself. He needs daddy Trump to come and support him." Other Talarico supporters said they believed Texas could turn blue. Jessica, from Lubbock, and Shelby, from Houston, cited dissatisfaction with how the state has been run in recent years. "I think they’re scared that it is going to flip, and I believe it will because of how they have run this county the last few years," they said. Christine and John, both from Lubbock, also predicted change. "They are nervous, and this is the year we are going to change it all," Christine said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Paloma, a Lubbock resident, put their optimism plainly: "This is the year that we flip blue. We are definitely going to flip the state."

articles.title: Dem AG’s ‘too many golf courses’ remark goes viral as critics tee off
articles.summary: Arizona Senate president Warren Petersen slammed Kris Mayes after she said the state has "too many golf courses" during a water conservation debate.
articles.body: Arizona’s Senate president took aim at viral comments about the future of golf from the state’s Democratic attorney general as their battle to be the state’s top law enforcement officer entered its final stretch before next week’s midterm elections. A remark about potentially restricting golf courses and the Grand Canyon State having "too much grass" turned a debate over water conservation into a campaign flashpoint, with Sen. Warren Petersen accusing Attorney General Kris Mayes of targeting a multibillion-dollar industry in the desert state while Mayes later insisted her remarks were taken out of context. "Kris Mayes thinks Arizona has too many golf courses. I think Arizona has too many radical politicians who believe government should dictate which industries get to thrive," Petersen, R-Maricopa, told Fox News Digital Tuesday. 100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE "Our golf courses support jobs, tourism, small businesses and communities across this state. Instead of attacking an industry that contributes to our economy, the attorney general should be focused on enforcing the law, protecting consumers and defending Arizona families." In an interview with Politico delving into the data center debate and whether the proliferation of water-intensive buildings is wise, particularly in an arid state, Mayes cited neighboring states allegedly "backed by" the Trump administration as hindrances to Arizona’s local supply. Mayes' golf course remarks came shortly after she warned that Arizona was headed toward a potential Supreme Court showdown over Colorado River water supplies. "We could do a hell of a lot more when it comes to conservation," she said, citing tax incentives for catchment and removal of lawns. GRAND CANYON WATER PIPELINE DAMAGED AGAIN AS FLOODING COMPLICATES REPAIRS "We have way, way too much grass in Arizona. We probably, frankly — and I'm sure the golf industry is not going to like this when I say this — we probably have too many golf courses in Arizona right now." That remark sparked blowback from Petersen and many others. "We don’t have a golf course problem in Arizona. We have a dumocrat (sic) problem in Arizona," quipped Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz. "Kris Mayes is promising to get rid of golf courses. I promise to get rid of Kris Mayes," Petersen added in his own tweet. E-procurement software CEO Tom Spengler added that Arizona "honestly need[s] more golf courses." "Tee times are very hard to get and rates have doubled or tripled since COVID," he said. "We have too much grass — said no one ever, other than Kris Mayes," added Turning Point USA executive Justin Streiff. Arizona’s business community also took notice, and Arizona Chamber of Commerce Vice President Courtney Coolidge responded to Mayes with several statistics about golf’s impact on the state. Coolidge reported a $6 billion economic impact, 66,000 jobs, $2.3 billion in wages and $520 million in tax revenue. Most relevant to the water debate, she said golf courses collectively use 2% or less of the state’s water resources. Those stats also lined up closely with separate figures in a 2023 study by the Arizona Alliance for Golf. Popular golf satire site PGA Tuor shared a clip of Mayes’ comments, writing, "How to not get re-elected 101." Another putting enthusiast said Mayes’ comments cost her his vote, saying, "[She] has no idea what the economic impact golf has on our entire state." Fox News Digital reached out to Mayes for comment on the viral nature and content of her remarks. The Democrat separately tweeted that she was intending to make a larger point about water usage. "Relax, nobody's closing golf courses," Mayes said. "My point is we need incentives to help all Arizonans and major industries swap thirsty grass and catch rainwater, especially if our water situation gets worse — while I take on the foreign mega-farms and data centers draining our water." She then accused Petersen of spreading "false claims." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But Mayes’ response was also met with ridicule. X critics called it "condescending" while one also quipped, "you relax – we all heard you." Others characterized her stated approach toward the golf industry as "communist." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With Election Day just days away, Petersen is betting the controversy will resonate beyond the fairways, casting Mayes' remarks as part of a larger dispute over government intervention in Arizona's economy as Republicans seek to regain control of a state government they once reliably held.

articles.title: Maharashtra MLC polls: Mahayuti wins 2 seats, NCP-SP clinches 2 for MVA
articles.summary: Maharashtra MLC polls: Mahayuti and MVA win 2 seats each; Nagpur graduates’ seat heads for a cliffhanger as BJP-Congress counting drags on.
articles.body: PUNE: Mahayuti and MVA won two seats each across the five graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies in Maharashtra legislative council elections, while the Nagpur graduates’ constituency emerged as the most dramatic contest, with the result hanging in the balance at the time of going to the press even though Congress claimed victory.The overall results exposed fault lines within the BJP-Shiv Sena-NCP Mahayuti, which failed to function as a cohesive alliance across the five constituencies.While BJP secured one seat, its partner Sena bagged another and NCP didn’t win any.Despite entering the polls as favourites, Mahayuti partners were mired in disagreements over seat-sharing, creating openings that Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) successfully exploited to secure two key contests.In a cliffhanger at Nagpur’s Mankapur Sports Complex, BJP’s Sudhakar Kohale and Congress candidate Abhijit Wanjarri traded leads through the day as counting stretched beyond 40 hours.Wanjarri surged ahead in the initial rounds before Kohale clawed his way back. With successive rounds narrowing the gap, both camps remained on edge as the final count progressed.The contest carried significance beyond a single seat. For BJP, it was a chance to reclaim a constituency it had dominated since the Jan Sangh era.For Congress, retaining the seat would reinforce its 2020 breakthrough, when Wanjarri defeated BJP’s Sandip Joshi. The battle was widely seen as a test of organisational strength in a region long regarded as a BJP bastion.Even before the final result, Kohale signalled acceptance of a possible defeat.Questioning the effectiveness of the voting process in graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies, he said, “Going by the trends in the last few rounds, it appears that the result may tilt in favour of the Congress candidate. Whatever the result, I am ready to accept it and will continue to carry out whatever responsibilities my party assigns to me.”Maharashtra Congress took a dig at chief minister Devendra Fadnavis over the Nagpur MLC seat, claiming that he had to delete a post from his own X account, in which he had stated that the Congress had won “zero” seats.“Devendraji posted a message in such haste that he later had to delete it. But remember, you can delete a tweet, not the truth,” the state Congress said in a post on its official X account.Cracks within partners cost MahayutiAmong Mahayuti’s victories, BJP’s Kaustubh Gawade won the Pune teachers’ constituency, defeating Shiv Sena rebel Sachin Sanap. In Amravati teachers’ constituency, Shiv Sena’s Kiran Sarnaik overcame Congress candidate Aditi Pohare and Sena rebel Shrikant Deshpande.The MVA’s victories came through NCP (SP). Harshada Deshmukh-Jadhav won the Pune graduates’ seat by defeating BJP’s Smita Jadhav, while Pratapsinh Patil unseated three-term MLC Satish Chavan in the Aurangabad graduates’ constituency.Political analyst Prakash Pawar said the outcome reflected BJP’s miscalculation during seat-sharing talks.“The election results revealed that even though BJP remains the most dominant party in the state, it has yet to secure organic support across all sections of society. The party tried to use its dominance to dictate seat-sharing arrangements and contest the polls without the support of its alliance partners but failed to garner sufficient support. It will have to rework its strategy in the state before facing the next elections,” he said.Senior BJP leader and cabinet minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule rejected suggestions that the results represented a setback. “The five seats were previously held by opposition parties, and we had no seats. Unlike the opposition parties, whenever we face a setback, we introspect and rework our strategy to win next time,” he said.Observers pointed particularly to western Maharashtra, where Mahayuti’s seat-sharing formula left NCP with no constituency to contest in the Pune division.“NCP has traditionally been strong there, but Mahayuti gave Sunetra Pawar’s NCP no seats in the Pune division, with both constituencies going to BJP. As a result, NCP workers did not campaign actively for Mahayuti candidates and were disappointed that their party did not get a ticket,” political analyst Pawar said.Shiv Sena workers were also conspicuously absent from BJP’s Pune campaign. Chief minister Eknath Shinde-led Sena even backed rebel candidates contesting against BJP-supported nominees in the teachers’ constituency.Former MLA and Shiv Sena’s Pune chief Ravindra Dhangekar raised concerns over the role of money in the elections.“We suspect that money power played a dominant role in the elections, which is quite unfortunate. In elections to graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies, we expect deserving candidates to be given tickets. Unfortunately, political parties have taken centre stage instead of the candidates, which is wrong,” he said.Boost for NCP (SP), introspection for alliesNCP (SP) state president Shashikant Shinde described the outcome as a morale booster.“The election results will be a turning point for our party, as they will send positive signals to our party workers ahead of the next elections. The results also underline the fact that when qualified candidates are nominated, voters support them,” he said.At the same time, he admitted that better coordination within the opposition alliance could have yielded more victories.“We should have started coordinating with our alliance partners much earlier for these elections, and we could have won more seats. The lack of coordination has cost us some seats,” he said.State Congress chief Harshwardhan Sapkal said his party had fought hard in the constituencies it contested and flagged the issue of invalid votes.“Our party contested three seats and made every effort to win. The counting process revealed that a large number of votes were declared invalid, which is a matter of concern,” he said.‘Wake-up call’ for NCP: Praful PatelThe verdict also triggered soul-searching within NCP after the defeat of senior leader Satish Chavan in the Aurangabad graduates’ constituency.NCP working president Praful Patel termed the result a warning signal and called for sweeping organisational reforms. In a social media post, Patel said: “The election results serve as a definitive wake-up call. The time has come for urgent introspection to rebuild trust, realign our priorities and fix our organisational structure. To regain people’s trust, reset the party’s priorities and bring about organisational reforms, an immediate and rigorous self-examination will be necessary.”(With inputs from Vaibhav Ganjapure and Abhishek Choudhari in Nagpur)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Frank Thorp V and Ryan Nobles speak with Democratic candidates who are touting their gun credentials. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into President Donald Trump’s potential next moves on Iran. — Adam Wollner Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights By Frank Thorp V and Ryan Nobles A group of Democratic candidates on the ballot next week are hoping to start a new conversation around guns as part of a strategy to win back rural voters in red-leaning areas. Wisconsin’s 1st District: Democrat Mitchell Berman’s ads have portrayed him as a proud gun owner and hunter. One shows him fishing while wearing a handgun in a holster; another shows him skeet-shooting with clay pigeons labeled “Data Centers.” After the target explodes in the air, his 6-year-old daughter yells, “Great shot, Dad!” “That’s who I am,” Berman told NBC News. “When I go fishing up north — where I’m from we have wolves. We have — in spring trout season, we have bears that are coming out of their dens with cubs. We’ve even had a mountain lion on our trail camera. So, you know, when I go out into the woods, I carry a sidearm with me for protection.” His race against GOP Rep. Bryan Steil was not expected to be close. President Donald Trump carried the district in 2020 and 2024, and Steil won re-election two years ago by 10 points. But polling has shown the race is within reach for Democrats. Texas’ 15th District: Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer turned Democratic congressional candidate, is not shy about his love for guns and hunting. He’s posted videos of him shooting a target a mile away, and his rec room is lined with the trophies he’s gathered on hunts. He even named his oldest son Remington. “Listen, in the rural areas, firearms are a way of life,” Pulido told NBC News, saying that fundraisers in the Rio Grande Valley are more common at skeet shooting events than at golf courses. Pulido is also running in an area that Trump won in the last two presidential elections. The district was redrawn earlier this year to make it more favorable for Republicans, but a shift in the Latino vote away from Trump mixed with a struggling economy has put Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz at risk of losing her bid for re-election. Read more → The big decision awaiting Trump after the midterms Analysis by Andrea Mitchell On the campaign trail, President Donald Trump has been confidently promising that oil prices will drop like a rock after the midterms — especially skyrocketing diesel fuel critical in farm states that could decide which party wins the Senate. Implicit is that he will attempt to do something decisive after next week to end the war against Iran and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. His not-so-subtle hints are backed up by new reporting in The Wall Street Journal and other publications that the U.S. has told Gulf partners it will resume intense, brief strikes against Iran after the midterms. And Israel’s hawkish Trump ally Benjamin Netanyahu has at least temporarily retained a caretaker role as prime minister while he and his rival, former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, jockey for a majority. In Israel’s complex parliamentary system, a decisive outcome could take weeks or months, or even lead to another election. That places Netanyahu in control of a potential resumption of the war, a position he had advocated for before Israelis went to the polls, according to The New York Times and other outlets. According to those reports, Israel’s military and intelligence leaders effectively vetoed that option, saying it would politicize their decision-making. As flawed as Israel’s democracy has been in many respects, according to many of its own citizens and even many longtime U.S. supporters, it still has the virtue of a largely independent military. But in the U.S., critics fear that may not be the case with the civilian leadership of the military in the second Trump administration. In past administrations in both political parties, secretaries of defense and their top deputies were usually experienced foreign policy or former military leaders, willing to offer independent opinions to the presidents they served in a formalized National Security Council inter-agency system. Conflicting options were debated in a deliberative process before they were presented to the commander in chief. Yes, on occasion, chief executives were misled by false narratives, like those delivered during the Vietnam War by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. Or, during the Iraq quagmire, when the chain of command was short-circuited by a powerful personality like President George W. Bush’s defense secretary, Donald Rumsfeld. Notably, Rumsfeld was forced out of his role the morning after Bush’s party got hammered in the 2006 midterms. Now, whether his party wins or loses in next week’s midterms, Trump faces what could be the most consequential decision of his second term: Whether to “finish the job” and resume attacking Iran. Such a decision would fly in the face of European leaders who counsel that renewed strikes would lead to higher oil prices, a potential economic downturn, and not produce a more compliant regime in Tehran. At the same time, there is now a growing consensus in Riyadh and other Gulf capitals that they need to find some accommodation with Iran in order to get the regime to try to restrain its Houthi proxies, who threaten to become an existential threat to their economies. The question for Trump is whether to follow the advice of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the former Fox News personality who has purged many of the Pentagon’s most experienced top generals and has privately advocated for resuming military action against Iran. The hawks could be right that a weakened Iran could be felled by a decisive blow, though skeptics note that such a strategy has not yet proved successful. The U.S. and global economy — to say nothing of Trump’s legacy — may well depend on what he decides in the next few weeks. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.standfirst: El portavoz de ERC recuerda el caso de Adamuz, cuando pasó algo similar
articles.summary: El portavoz de ERC recuerda el caso de Adamuz, cuando pasó algo similar
articles.body: El accidente ferroviario de Urda, en Toledo, que ha paralizado los trenes entre Madrid y Andalucía, ha traído consigo no solo decenas de muertos y heridos, también un aumento de precios en los billetes de avión para poder viajar, algo que ya ocurrió en el accidente de Adamuz (Córdoba). Eso sí, desde Iberia han intentado evitar esto subiendo un 20% la capacidad de asientos entre Madrid y Andalucía, lo que son 520 plazas adicionales, gracias a la utilización de los modelos Airbus A321. Además, este miércoles, 28 de octubre, habrá dos vuelos adicionales entre Madrid y Málaga. Además, la aerolínea ha establecido un límite máximo en sus tarifas hasta el domingo 8 de noviembre, fijando los billetes en un tope de 99 euros por trayecto en clase Turista y 149 euros en Business. Sin embargo, esta medida no ha sido suficiente para muchos, como es el caso de Gabriel Rufián, que ha acudido a su cuenta de X para criticar la situación y que esto no pueda frenarse desde el Gobierno. El portavoz de ERC (Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya) en el Congreso no dudó en publicar este post: “Sigue siendo mucho dinero y durante muy poco tiempo. Tras el accidente de Adamuz un vuelo de Madrid a Málaga pasó de costar 40 a 400€. Y vuelve a pasar lo mismo. Hay que legislar para que ninguna empresa pueda hacer negocio durante una emergencia así. La mano invisible del mercado sin control siempre acaba en el cuello del consumidor”. Y es que, en Adamuz, el accidente sufrido el pasado mes de enero, los vuelos a Andalucía se multiplicaron en hasta un 400%, según los datos aportados por el portal de Google Flights, algo que ha vuelto a ocurrir este miércoles de octubre.
