articles.title: Stevens’s fiance says he’ll vote for Rogers over El-Sayed
articles.summary: The fiance of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) said this week he would support GOP candidate Mike Rogers over Stevens’s former Democratic primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan’s Senate race. In an interview published Wednesday, Jason Turkish accused the Democrat of using antisemitic language on the campaign trail. “We have never seen a candidate for U.S.…
articles.body:
The fiance of Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) said this week he would support GOP candidate Mike Rogers over Stevens’s former Democratic primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan’s Senate race.

In an interview published Wednesday, Jason Turkish accused the Democrat of using antisemitic language on the campaign trail.

“We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul,” the Jewish Democratic donor told The Detroit News .

Stevens and Turkish announced their engagement in August, after El-Sayed narrowly defeated the House member in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. Stevens publicly backed El-Sayed after this loss, but she has not campaigned alongside him in several months.

Turkish told The Detroit News he has witnessed “an escalation in his [El-Sayed’s] rhetoric since the primary, and it makes folks unsafe.”

“Every time he talks about genocide, Jews get death threats,” he continued.

El-Sayed apologized in August for comments he made after an attack on a Detroit-area synagogue.

He has also faced scrutiny for his broader criticism of the Israeli government over its military operations in Gaza and distanced himself from Hasan Piker after the left-wing Twitch streamer, who joined El-Sayed on the campaign trail, made controversial comments about American Jews who support Israel.

In a statement to The Detroit News, the Democrat’s campaign spokesperson, Roxie Richner, said El-Sayed was “focused on building a broad coalition” in the state.

Turkish said he plans to attend a Rogers campaign event in Birmingham, Mich., on Wednesday evening hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition. The event, titled “Who Will Keep Us Safe? Rogers vs. El-Sayed,” will feature the GOP nominee and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

Turkish’s announcement follows a recent declaration from Stevens’s former campaign chair to Jewish Insider on Tuesday that he would similarly not support El-Sayed in the November race.

“I have lots of issues with Mike Rogers, and I’m not even willing to use words like ‘support,’” David Kramer told the outlet. “But I’ve made peace with voting for him because I do think that he at least does care about Jews being safe and participating in public life, and he seems to know the difference between an enemy of ours in Iran and an ally of ours [in Israel].”

The Hill has reached out to El-Sayed’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: Murkowski calls for ‘truth’ from Peltola amid ‘pattern of lies and coverups’
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) called for the “truth” from former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) amid what she said was a “pattern of lies and coverups” following reports the Democrat’s campaign recruited one of her midterm opponents to “ballot-stack.” “While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) called for the “truth” from former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) amid what she said was a “pattern of lies and coverups” following reports the Democrat’s campaign recruited one of her midterm opponents to “ballot-stack.”

“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski wrote in a statement to The Hill. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments.”

The senator continued that “by contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”

“Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign—what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials,” she concluded.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Peltola’s campaign, alongside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), attempted to recruit one of her opponents who shared the same name as the GOP’s incumbent candidate: Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC have denied being involved with the effort.

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC. and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” the Peltola campaign said in a statement earlier Wednesday.

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s mere presence on the ballot has angered the Justice Department, which filed a lawsuit earlier this month, attempting to block certification of the election if the incumbent senator loses. Alaska’s GOP-led government urged a federal court to dismiss the case Wednesday.

Murkowski previously advocated against the lawsuit, expressing on social media , “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.”

“The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit,” she added.

Though the alleged tactics are not illegal, President Trump stated he believed Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate.

“I think the fake Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola, number one they should be taken off the ballot, and number two they should be prosecuted,” the president articulated on Truth Social.

articles.title: El-Sayed rallygoers urge 'major change,' cash handouts to fight cost crisis
articles.summary: Supporters of Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed praised his Medicare for All and other progressive platforms at a Detroit rally.
articles.body: DETROIT — Supporters of Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told Fox News Digital the Great Lake State is due for a progressive champion and person of color in statewide office. "I personally think he's resonating with people in Michigan because he is a person of color, obviously, and then, secondly, he gets down, and he's 10 toes down," said Emily Walker, a teacher at Cass Technical High School, the venue where El-Sayed hosted a rally on Saturday. "He's out here with the people. He's knocking on doors. He's talking to the community," Walker added. "He's also a medical professional, and I just feel like he's very educated, and he understands what's going on in policies." OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Fox News Digital spoke with voters outside Cass Technical High School, where El-Sayed hosted a campaign rally featuring former President Barack Obama Saturday. Obama’s appearance alongside El-Sayed became a major event as the progressive candidate continues working to consolidate backing across the Democratic Party spectrum ahead of the November general election against Republican nominee Mike Rogers. While exiting the overflow venue, supporters were asked for their thoughts on guaranteed income programs and whether candidates should campaign for them. AS AMERICANS ARE CRUSHED BY AFFORDABILITY, GROWING TREND OF MAYORS PUSHING CASH HANDOUTS AS THE ANSWER "I think we need a major change in what we have with Donald Trump and his cohorts," said Dave, an attendee at the event. "The Democrats, I don't think, have been listening well enough. I think we need to change big time instead of just slowly." Kiana Montgomery, a publicist attending the rally, agreed that El-Sayed's message aligns with what local voters are seeking. "I think he won because he is speaking to the things that are important to people: education, healthcare and bringing down the costs that are going on right now," Montgomery said. "People are trying to do more than just exist. They're trying to thrive, and they're unable to do that in the economic times right now." El-Sayed’s campaign platform centers heavily on universal healthcare through Medicare-for-all, raising the federal minimum wage and expanding social safety net initiatives. He has also voiced support for guaranteed income program, government-distributed financial assistance provided without strings attached, to support residents during economic hardship or pregnancy. VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE Jamal Jenkins told Fox News Digital progressive proposals are finding traction because voters want tangible action on the cost of living. "I think a progressive is resonating because people want to see more action towards putting a dent into affordability," Jenkins said. "When you look at corporate profits and the wealth gap between the wealthy, the shrinking middle class and the impoverished, I think folks want to see action. So, more people are actively participating in a positive way in the economy and can live a dignified life. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE "I think everybody wants the same thing for themselves and for their kids," Jenkins added. "Just to have a shot at an education, a good life, work-life balance and to live life without having to struggle as much for reasons that really don't make much sense." El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former Wayne County health director, has made expanding healthcare coverage a central focus of his bid to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. He has consistently championed Medicare-for-all to create a government-funded health coverage system. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS TRUMP DOMINATES EL-SAYED'S ATTACKS AGAINST ROGERS, BUT GOP RIVAL OFFERS UNEXPECTED POLICY SPLIT Mohammed, a resident of Bloomfield Hills, said El-Sayed brings fresh perspective to economic and foreign policy discussions. "The old way of doing business isn't working anymore," Mohammed said. "We don't want to see our money being taken away from us. We want to see our money being used for the children here, for the elderly here and for those in need. With our grocery prices and gas prices being the way they are, we shouldn't be fighting stupid wars anymore, as he keeps saying. "I think for all of us as citizens of Michigan, he's a better fit because he's looking out for us as opposed to big pharma and PACs." El-Sayed has bristled at media questions about his criticism of Israel, which has become a mainstream position in the Democratic Party, saying it distracts from issues voters want to talk about. articles.title: Justice Department pushes to keep Ilhan Omar search warrant under seal for now
articles.summary: Federal prosecutors asked a judge Tuesday to reject a request from more than a dozen news organizations to immediately unseal the search warrant for Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) Washington, D.C., home, saying it could jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation. A heavily redacted filing signed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia,…
articles.body:
Federal prosecutors asked a judge Tuesday to reject a request from more than a dozen news organizations to immediately unseal the search warrant for Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) Washington, D.C., home, saying it could jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation .

A heavily redacted filing signed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, argues that the media’s request is premature because the warrant has not yet been fully executed and no decision on charges has been announced.

“Unsealing everything now imperils the investigation, and publicly exposes suspected criminal wrongdoing against which may yet mount a defense in court,” the prosecutors wrote.

Pirro’s office noted that it does not oppose unsealing some of the redacted documents later “so the public can see how the legal process played out,” but urged the judge to hold off for now.

“The Search Warrant Records need not remain sealed indefinitely,” prosecutors wrote. “The United States trusts that, with the Court’s help, the warrant will be fully executed soon, and it anticipates that a public charging decision will follow.”

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, an Obama appointee who serves as the chief judge on the federal bench in D.C., is overseeing the case.

It was brought by 14 news organizations three days after federal agents raided Omar’s Washington home as part of a criminal probe into alleged immigration fraud. The congresswoman has since said she intends to move out of the apartment due to death threats.

The scope of the investigation has not been made public, but reports indicate it is focused on accusations that Omar’s father may have lied about her age on immigration paperwork. Omar was around 12 years old when her family came to the U.S. from Somalia and obtained U.S. citizenship in 2000.

The news organizations called for “maximum transparency” in their request to the judge, arguing that the “enormous public interest and historic significance” outweigh “any potential interest in their continued secrecy.”

The timing of the search drew scrutiny, as the Justice Department typically refrains from taking major actions against candidates for office close to an election. Omar is seeking her fifth term in the House.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote on social media after the raid. “For ten years, [President] Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

articles.title: 10 eleitos em 2026 acumulam R$ 5,7 milhões em condenações no TCU | G1
articles.standfirst: Políticos foram eleitos deputados estaduais, deputado federal e suplente de senador. Irregularidades envolvem recursos destinados a áreas como educação, saúde, cultura e assistência social, incluindo alimentação escolar, unidades de saúde, eventos culturais e qualificação profissional de jovens.
articles.summary: Políticos eleitos com contas irregulares somam R$ 5,7 milhões em condenações no TCU por falhas na gestão de verbas da saúde, educação e assistência social.
articles.body:
10 eleitos já tiveram contas julgaras irregulares pelo TCU em cargos anteriores. — Foto: Arte g1

Levantamento do g1 identificou que dez políticos eleitos em 2026 tiveram contas julgadas irregulares pelo Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) por problemas na aplicação de recursos públicos em cargos anteriores.

As condenações financeiras somam quase R$ 5,7 milhões, entre valores a serem devolvidos aos cofres públicos e multas. O levantamento considerou apenas decisões do TCU que responsabilizaram pessoalmente os políticos, excluindo casos em que a obrigação de devolver os recursos foi atribuída às prefeituras, por exemplo. O cálculo não inclui juros e correção monetária. Em alguns casos, as quantias já foram quitadas ou estão sendo pagas em parcelas.

As irregularidades vão da falta de prestação de contas e de comprovação de pagamentos a obras inacabadas, problemas na contratação de artistas e suspeitas sobre realização de cursos profissionalizantes.

Os casos foram identificados em 15 processos relacionados ao uso de recursos federais em municípios de diferentes estados do país. A maior parte das verbas foi repassada por meio de convênios com o governo federal. Os demais processos envolvem recursos destinados a programas nacionais de educação, saúde e assistência social.

A maioria dos políticos ocupava o cargo de prefeito quando ocorreram as irregularidades. Há também um ex-secretário municipal de Infraestrutura e um ex-presidente de associação de municípios.

🔎Os nomes constam na relação do TCU de gestores públicos com contas julgadas irregulares para fins eleitorais. Ela é utilizada pela Justiça Eleitoral para auxiliar a análise dos pedidos de registro de candidatura, mas ter o nome na lista não significa que a pessoa esteja automaticamente impedida de disputar eleições. Cabe à Justiça Eleitoral analisar os requisitos para eventual inelegibilidade.

A relação reúne casos com decisões definitivas nos últimos oito anos e inclui situações de omissão na prestação de contas, uso indevido de recursos públicos e desvio de dinheiro ou bens públicos, entre outras irregularidades.

Sede do Tribunal de cotnas da União (TCU), em Brasília. — Foto: Divulgação/TCU

Não entraram no levantamento o nome de pessoas que ainda não foram notificados das decisões, decisões que ainda admitem recurso, julgamentos anulados ou suspensos pelo TCU ou pela Justiça e condenações ao pagamento de multa, sem que haja condenação a devolução de recursos também.

Quando a condenação é definitiva e a quantia não é paga, o TCU pode encaminhar o caso à Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), responsável por adotar medidas de cobrança judicial ou extrajudicial. Segundo o órgão, em 2026, foram encaminhados 1.784 títulos para cobrança. No mesmo período, a AGU arrecadou R$ 57,7 milhões, incluindo débitos e multas.

R$ 4 milhões de recursos públicos a serem devolvidos

Do total das condenações identificadas, aproximadamente R$ 4 milhões correspondem a valores que o TCU determinou devolver aos cofres públicos. Já as multas aplicadas somam cerca de R$ 1,6 milhão. O valor dessa penalidade varia conforme a natureza das irregularidades e pode chegar a 100% do valor do dano causado aos cofres públicos.

No Pará, Elias Santiago (PT-PA), eleito deputado estadual, teve as contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na utilização de recursos do Programa Nacional de Alimentação Escolar (PNAE), durante sua gestão como prefeito de Concórdia do Pará, em 2011.

O TCU reconheceu que não foram encontradas evidências de desvio dos recursos, mas encontrou outras falhas na execução do programa, como diferenças entre os valores movimentados nas contas bancárias do programa e as despesas declaradas. O valor para devolver aos cofres públicos foi definido em R$ 14.233,14, com multa de R$ 10 mil.

Também no Pará, Rui Begot (Pode-PA), eleito deputado estadual, teve contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na aplicação de recursos do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), destinados ao Programa Expansão da Saúde da Família (Proesf) em Ananindeua, nos exercícios de 2003 e 2004.

Na época, ele era secretário municipal de Infraestrutura e foi responsabilizado por confirmar a execução de serviços não realizados. A fiscalização identificou materiais adquiridos que não foram encontrados nas unidades de saúde e pagamentos por serviços de construção não executados ou não comprovados.

Rui foi condenado a devolver R$ 13.982,60, juntamente com a ex-secretária municipal de Saúde Antônia Lúcia da Silva Palheta Ferreira. Não houve aplicação de multa. Em março de 2025, o TCU reconheceu que o débito havia sido integralmente pago e concedeu quitação aos dois responsáveis, mas o nome dele seguirá na lista do TCU até maio de 2029.

No Piauí, Janaínna Marques (PT-PI), eleita deputada estadual, teve as contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na aplicação de recursos dos programas Nacional de Apoio ao Transporte do Escolar (PNATE) e Dinheiro Direto na Escola (PDDE), durante sua gestão como prefeita de Luzilândia, em 2006.

A fiscalização identificou pagamentos a diferentes fornecedores por meio de um único cheque e divergências nos saldos bancários, o que dificultou a comprovação da utilização dos recursos. O TCU determinou o ressarcimento de R$ 135.543,27 e multa de R$ 25 mil. Jannaína já havia devolvido R$ 30.083,78 em 2015, e o valor foi abatido da dívida.

Elias Santiago, Rui Begot e Jannaína Marques foram procurados, mas não responderam.

Em Mato Grosso, Cidinho Santos (PP-MT), eleito primeiro suplente de senador, teve as contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na execução do convênio firmado entre o Ministério do Turismo e a Associação Mato-Grossense dos Municípios (AMM), da qual era presidente. O recurso era para o projeto Fomento à Cultura e ao Turismo Mato-Grossense.

A fiscalização identificou inconsistências na comprovação de um show da dupla Edson & Hudson, incluindo divergências nas datas do evento e questionamentos sobre a empresa responsável pela apresentação. Ele foi condenado a devolver cerca de R$ 146 mil, e à multa de R$ 25 mil.

Em resposta ao g1 , a defesa de Cidinho Santos afirmou que os valores determinados pelo TCU foram integralmente devolvidos e que a multa foi paga. Segundo o advogado Rodrigo Cyrineu, não há pendência financeira nem processo em andamento sobre o caso, encerrado e arquivado pelo Tribunal em julho de 2021.

No Rio Grande do Sul, o ex-prefeito de São Lourenço do Sul Zé Nunes (PT), eleito deputado estadual, teve contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na utilização de recursos do Ministério do Turismo destinados à realização da 26ª edição do Reponte da Canção, evento cultural do município.

A fiscalização identificou irregularidades na contratação de artistas por meio de empresas intermediárias, sem comprovação de que elas detinham exclusividade para representar as atrações. Também não foram apresentados documentos suficientes para comprovar o pagamento dos cachês.

Em 2021, o TCU condenou Zé Nunes a devolver R$ 47.385 e aplicou multas que somam R$ 14 mil. Procurada pelo g1, a defesa informou que os valores estão sendo pagos de forma parcelada, em acordo com a União.

No Rio Grande do Norte, Francisco do PT (PT-RN), eleito deputado estadual, teve contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na aplicação de recursos federais destinados ao 14º Arraiá da Zona Sul, realizado em Parelhas, município que administrou como prefeito.

Assim como no caso de Zé Nunes, o TCU apontou falhas na contratação de artistas e falta de documentos que comprovassem o pagamento dos cachês aos músicos. Francisco foi condenado a devolver R$ 63 mil aos cofres públicos, além de pagar multa de R$ 10 mil.

Recursos para saúde e assistência social

Na Bahia, Diego Coronel (Republicanos-BA), eleito deputado federal, teve contas julgadas irregulares por problemas na aplicação de recursos do Fundo Nacional de Assistência Social (FNAS) em 2012, quando era prefeito de Coração de Maria.

A fiscalização identificou despesas sem documentação suficiente para comprovar o uso dos recursos nos programas de Proteção Social Básica e Proteção Social Especial, além de pagamentos para finalidades diferentes das previstas. Em 2021, o TCU condenou Diego a devolver R$ 30.094,07 aos cofres públicos e aplicou multa de R$ 10 mil.

Em resposta ao g1 , o advogado Odilon Santos afirmou que Diego Coronel está cumprindo a determinação do TCU por meio de parcelamento, com pagamentos em dia.

A defesa também informou que os mesmos fatos foram analisados em uma ação de improbidade administrativa na Justiça Federal, julgada improcedente por decisão definitiva. Segundo o advogado, o próprio Ministério Público Federal pediu a improcedência da ação após analisar as provas. A decisão judicial, contudo, não anula automaticamente a condenação administrativa do TCU.

Em Alagoas, o ex-prefeito Cícero Cavalcanti (MDB-AL), eleito deputado estadual, teve contas julgadas irregulares em dois processos relacionados ao uso de recursos federais da Fundação Nacional de Saúde (Funasa) durante sua gestão em São Luís do Quitunde.

O primeiro envolveu verbas destinadas à reconstrução de 95 unidades habitacionais para prevenção da doença de Chagas. A fiscalização identificou obras parcialmente executadas, pagamentos por serviços não realizados e falhas na prestação de contas.

Cícero foi responsabilizado por uma transferência bancária de R$ 9 mil sem comprovação de vínculo com o convênio e pelo pagamento de R$ 9.038,88 por serviços não executados. Neste último caso, a responsabilidade foi atribuída também à empresa Eficaz Construções. O TCU determinou a devolução de R$ 18.038,88 e aplicou multa de R$ 3 mil.

O segundo processo envolveu recursos para ampliar o sistema de abastecimento de água do município. Embora os R$ 160 mil previstos tenham sido integralmente pagos à empresa contratada, fiscalizações da Funasa constataram que apenas 2% dos serviços haviam sido executados.

Em 2018, o TCU determinou a devolução integral dos R$ 160 mil, mas não aplicou multa devido à prescrição do prazo para essa penalidade. Procurado pelo g1 , Cícero Cavalcanti não respondeu.

Contas irregulares em três processos diferentes

Entre os dez políticos identificados no levantamento, Fábio Henrique (MDB-SE) e Osni Cardoso (PT-BA), eleitos deputados estaduais, tiveram contas julgadas irregulares em três processos cada um. As irregularidades ocorreram quando os dois exerciam o cargo de prefeito.

As três condenações financeiras de Fábio Henrique estão relacionadas à sua gestão em Nossa Senhora do Socorro (SE). O primeiro processo envolve recursos destinados à modernização das feiras livres do município.

A fiscalização identificou balanças com características diferentes das previstas no projeto e falta de documentos que comprovassem a entrega de jalecos aos feirantes. O TCU determinou a devolução de R$ 55.409,30 aos cofres públicos e aplicou multa de R$ 10 mil.

Os outros dois processos envolvem o Projovem Trabalhador, programa financiado pelo Ministério do Trabalho para oferecer qualificação profissional a jovens. Em um deles, a prefeitura contratou, sem licitação, a Agência de Tecnologia, Pesquisa e Ensino do Nordeste (ATNE) para oferecer cursos a 2 mil participantes.

Segundo a fiscalização, a entidade não tinha estrutura adequada para executar os serviços. Também foram identificados documentos falsificados, movimentações bancárias irregulares e falta de comprovação da realização das atividades.

O TCU condenou Fábio Henrique a devolver R$ 1.167.469,16, em responsabilidade conjunta com a ex-presidente da ATNE, Márcia Valéria Ferreira da Cruz, além de aplicar multa de R$ 350 mil ao ex-prefeito.

No terceiro processo, a prefeitura contratou a Tocqueville Organização da Sociedade Civil de Interesse Público para executar atividades do mesmo programa. O TCU apontou falta de comprovação da realização dos cursos, movimentações bancárias irregulares e documentação insuficiente para demonstrar a aplicação dos recursos.

Nesse caso, o tribunal determinou a devolução de R$ 1.411.487,94, em responsabilidade conjunta com a Tocqueville, e aplicou multa de R$ 1 milhão a Fábio Henrique.

Em resposta ao g1, a defesa do ex-prefeito informou que tramita desde 2022 uma ação judicial para tentar anular as condenações do TCU. Segundo os advogados, houve um julgamento não unânime no Tribunal Regional Federal da 5ª Região (TRF5), e o caso está em fase de recurso no Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ).

Na Bahia, Osni Cardoso teve contas julgadas irregulares em três processos relacionados à sua gestão como prefeito de Serrinha. O primeiro envolve recursos do Programa Nacional de Alimentação Escolar (PNAE), referentes a 2015.

A fiscalização identificou pagamentos sem comprovação adequada e o uso de parte das verbas destinadas à alimentação dos estudantes para depósitos judiciais relacionados a dívidas do município. O TCU determinou a devolução de R$ 630.805,04 ao Fundo Nacional de Desenvolvimento da Educação (FNDE) e aplicou multa de R$ 150 mil.

Os outros dois processos envolvem recursos do Programa Brasil Alfabetizado, voltado à alfabetização de jovens, adultos e idosos. No primeiro, referente a 2010, o TCU constatou que a prefeitura não prestou contas dos R$ 53.235 repassados ao município. Osni foi condenado a devolver o valor e a pagar multa de R$ 10 mil.

O terceiro processo trata de R$ 105.072,35 transferidos ao município em 2013, cuja prestação de contas também não foi apresentada. O tribunal determinou a devolução integral da quantia e aplicou multa de R$ 20 mil.

Osni não respondeu aos contatos feitos pelo g1.

articles.title: Análise de dados, abstenções e estratégia nas redes: como campanha de Lula mudou rota no 2º turno e conseguiu virada inédita | G1
articles.standfirst: Campanha também reconhece que mobilização espontânea das ruas foi fundamental para vitória no segundo turno. Lula venceu o segundo turno após ter terminado o 1º turno atrás de Flávio.
articles.summary: Campanha também reconhece que mobilização espontânea das ruas foi fundamental para vitória no segundo turno. Lula venceu o segundo turno após ter terminado o 1º turno atrás de Flávio.
articles.body:
Após o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) ficar atrás de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no primeiro turno da disputa presidencial, a campanha petista recalculou a rota para o segundo turno.

Entre as mudanças, montou uma sala de situação no QG em Brasília, liderada pelo secretário de Organização do PT, Laércio Ribeiro de Oliveira.

O grupo, que também tinha entre os coordenadores o senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE) e o presidente do PT, Edinho Silva, além de uma equipe técnica, passou a analisar dados para definir estratégias específicas por região.

O objetivo era identificar onde a campanha deveria trabalhar para aumentar a rejeição a Flávio Bolsonaro, onde deveria intensificar mensagens positivas e a mobilização por Lula e onde uma atuação mais intensa poderia acabar mobilizando eleitores do adversário.

A diferença entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula no primeiro turno de eleição presidencial foi a menor já registrada desde a redemocratização . Com 100% das urnas apuradas, Flávio recebeu 47,03% dos votos válidos, enquanto o atual presidente teve 45,16%, uma distância de 1,87 ponto percentual, segundo dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Laércio Oliveira explica que, no primeiro turno, a campanha de Lula se organizou com o que tinham de experiência exitosa de 2022, quando Lula venceu Jair Bolsonaro.

Nessa primeira fase da campanha, a coordenação focou na montagem dos comitês de campanha e populares, com movimentos sociais, sindicatos e partidos da base.

"Somado a isso, a gente tinha a organização do Pode Espalhar, que era uma coisa montada em 2022, aprimorada um pouco, mas era orgânico, alcançava mais a militância. Tivemos o Porta-voz do presidente Lula, sob a coordenação do Boulos, para tentar ampliar o simpatizante que não era do PT, mas que era progressista, mas, na prática, esse engajamento só aconteceu no segundo turno com [André] Janones, que extrapolou a bolha", disse o secretário.

A sala de situação foi montada em 5 de outubro, um dia depois da eleição do primeiro turno, e era composta por seis integrantes na sala física e mais dez na central de relacionamento virtual com pessoas de diferentes estados.

Também houve mudança na coordenação nacional da campanha, com a entrada de três políticos nordestinos para tentar mudar os rumos das eleições no segundo turno :

O senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE), ex-ministro da Educação e ex-governador do Ceará, como coordenador político;

o senador eleito Rui Costa (PT-BA), ex-ministro da Casa Civil e ex-governador da Bahia, na coordenação da agenda;

e Rafael Fonteles (PT-PI), governador reeleito do Piauí, na coordenação da comunicação.

A partir daí, a campanha passou a destrinchar os dados disponibilizados pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral.

As análises buscavam identificar onde havia maior capacidade de mobilização com mensagens positivas, onde estava a maior concentração de eleitores de Lula, onde era preciso mobilizar quem havia se abstido e onde seria possível atuar para aumentar a rejeição ao adversário e desmobilizar o voto do outro lado.

A campanha também disponibilizava materiais separados por temas e objetivos de comunicação.

Nos locais em que a meta era ampliar a rejeição ao adversário, havia conteúdos específicos para essa finalidade. Onde a prioridade era aumentar a mobilização em torno de Lula, a orientação era usar mensagens mais positivas, com foco no futuro, por exemplo.

"Se você olhar o resultado do Brasil inteiro, o que mais surtiu efeito foi a redução da abstenção e o eleitor que voltou para a urna, não tinha ido no primeiro turno, foi para a urna ou que mesmo não tinha votado em 2022. Isso foi o que mais surtiu efeito, mas tem esse eleitor da terceira via, que foi para ele (Lula). São quase 10 milhões de votos, né?", disse Laércio.

Paralelamente a isso, o presidente Lula se aproximou de jovens eleitos no primeiro turno e foi convencido por Fonteles da importância de ter uma comunicação direta com os eleitores nas redes sociais.

O deputado federal André Janones abraça o presidente Lula, reeleito neste domingo — Foto: Rafael Peixoto/g1

Lula passou a gravar vídeos para as diferentes plataformas digitais , e a campanha começou a adotar a estratégia de mostrá-lo como estadista, como em vídeos direcionados a Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Pernambuco.

Junto aos movimentos das ruas e a presença de Lula nas redes sociais, foi se intensificando também a mobilização digital realizada pelo deputado federal André Janones (Rede-MG), com um estilo combativo que até então provocava resistência em setores do PT.

O deputado comandou o canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula", com 10,5 milhões de seguidores, e ensinou como usar os algoritmos para virar a eleição.

Para Laércio de Oliveira, a lição que as eleições deste ano deixa é que o modelo de organização e de fazer campanha tradicionais continuam tendo alguma importância, mas são insuficientes para ganhar uma disputa.

"Esse segundo turno mostrou que é preciso ter criatividade, que tem que falar de forma direta com a massa. Não tem mais intermediário. Você fala com o sindicato, o sindicato reproduz essa relação com os seus trabalhadores. Você fala com movimento social organizado, o movimento social organizado reproduz isso. Eu acho que a sociedade está mudando nesse sentido, está perdendo os intermediários", disse.

"Não significa que isso deixa de ter importância porque voocê organiza a luta, organiza a partir disso, as suas pautas, mas isso é insuficiente hoje para você falar com o povo, falar com a massa."

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: veja o que pode acontecer com o mandato de senador após fuga para os EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio foi eleito para o Senado em 2018, com 4.380.418 votos, sendo o candidato mais votado para o cargo no RJ. Mandato como senador vai até 31 de janeiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Flávio foi eleito para o Senado em 2018, com 4.380.418 votos, sendo o candidato mais votado para o cargo no RJ. Mandato como senador vai até 31 de janeiro de 2027.
articles.body:
A fuga do senador e candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) para os Estados Unidos levantou dúvidas sobre o futuro de seu mandato parlamentar. De acordo com as regras previstas na Constituição Federal e no Regimento Interno do Senado , a saída ou permanência no exterior não acarreta a perda automática da cadeira de senador.

Flávio desembarcou em Miami nesta quarta-feira (28), após deixar o Brasil e passar pela Argentina. O senador foi derrotado por Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no segundo turno da eleição presidencial, realizado no domingo (25).

Até o momento, Flávio Bolsonaro não fez nenhuma comunicação oficial ao Senado sobre sua saída do país nem formalizou qualquer pedido de licença ou afastamento do mandato.

Flávio Bolsonaro foi eleito para o Senado nas eleições de outubro de 2018, assumindo a cadeira em fevereiro de 2019. O parlamentar obteve 4.380.418 votos , sendo o candidato mais votado para o cargo no estado do Rio de Janeiro.

O mandato de senador de Flávio se estende até 31 de janeiro de 2027 .

Atualmente, Flávio recebe R$ 46.366,19 por mês como senador da República.

De acordo a Constituição Federal, o parlamentar pode perder o mandato se deixar de comparecer a um terço das sessões ordinárias de cada ano, exceto nos casos de licença ou de missão oficial autorizada.

Nessa hipótese por excesso de ausências, a cassação não vai a votação no plenário; a perda do mandato é declarada pela Mesa Diretora do Senado. Além disso, ausências não justificadas em sessões deliberativas podem gerar descontos diretos na remuneração mensal.

Para evitar a contagem de faltas, o senador pode solicitar uma licença para tratar de interesses particulares, que pode durar até 120 dias por sessão legislativa, sem remuneração .

Caso o pedido seja formalizado e aprovado dentro das normas do Senado, os dias de afastamento não são contabilizados como ausências não justificadas.

O candidato à presidência do Brasil, Flávio Bolsonaro, do Partido Liberal (PL), discursa após perder o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, em Brasília, Brasil, em 25 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Agustin Marcarian

Pelas regras do Senado, a convocação do suplente só ocorre em casos de vacância do cargo — como em situações de morte, renúncia ou cassação — ou em afastamentos por licença que ultrapassem 120 dias. Até o momento, não há registro de pedido formal de licença ou afastamento apresentado pelo senador.

A Constituição estabelece ainda que um senador também pode ter o mandato cassado se descumprir proibições do cargo, adotar conduta incompatível com o decoro parlamentar, tiver os direitos políticos suspensos, for condenado criminalmente em decisão definitiva (sem possibilidade de recurso) ou optar pela renúncia.

Nos casos de quebra de decoro, infrações regimentais ou condenação criminal, a perda do cargo não é automática.

O processo precisa ser provocado por senadores ou por partidos políticos com representação no Congresso e aprovado pela maioria absoluta do plenário, ou seja, pelo menos 41 parlamentares.

O senador pode exercer o mandato fora do Brasil?

O Regimento Interno do Senado estabelece que um senador deve comunicar ao presidente da Casa sempre que se ausentar do país. Nessa comunicação, o parlamentar também deve informar o prazo da ausência.

A simples permanência no exterior, portanto, não significa automaticamente renúncia ou perda do mandato.

A permanência do parlamentar no exterior não o impede tecnicamente de votar durante deliberações em formato remoto ou semipresencial. No entanto, a situação poderá ser revista, assim como foi feito na Câmara dos Deputados ( veja mais abaixo ).

O voto remoto no Senado não fica disponível de forma irrestrita aos parlamentares. Ele pode ser utilizado quando a sessão ou reunião permite participação remota, por meio de um sistema interno que é cadastrado no telefone dos parlamentares.

A norma prevê que o Senado pode funcionar de forma exclusivamente remota ou semipresencial em situações específicas, como força maior ou urgência devidamente justificada, ou mediante convocação previamente divulgada pelo presidente da Casa.

Nesses casos, senadores que estejam no exercício do mandato podem participar à distância e, nas votações nominais ostensivas, registrar o voto por meio do celular.

No entanto, quando a sessão é presencial, o uso do aplicativo para votação só é liberado para parlamentares que tenham registrado presença fisicamente no Congresso . O mecanismo permite a votação eletrônica fora do plenário — inclusive pelas dependências da Casa —, mas não isenta o senador de comparecer presencialmente.

Além disso, a votação à distância possui restrições regimentais: deliberações que exigem voto secreto ou presencial obrigatoriamente exigem o comparecimento físico ao Plenário ou às comissões.

Flávio usou a modalidade de voto remoto para votar a favor da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que colocou fim à escala de trabalho 6x1. Na ocasião, Flávio estava em um ato de campanha no momento da votação.

O movimento de viajar para os Estados Unidos e tentar exercer a atividade parlamentar do exterior não é inédito no Congresso . A estratégia já foi adotada pelo deputado cassado Eduardo Bolsonaro, irmão de Flávio, que deixou o Brasil durante o mandato e tentou, sem sucesso, dar continuidade aos trabalhos na Câmara de forma remota.

Após se mudar para o exterior, Eduardo tirou uma licença do mandato de 120 dias . Após o prazo se encerrar, o parlamentar chegou a solicitar autorização para exercer o mandato de forma remota , alegando perseguição política.

No entanto, as regras do Congresso Nacional não preveem a atuação parlamentar contínua a partir do exterior.

Em novembro de 2025, durante uma sessão conjunta do Congresso, Eduardo tentou registrar seu voto pelo aplicativo enquanto estava nos EUA , mas o registro acabou anulado pela presidência da Mesa Diretora por descumprir as normas vigentes.

Devido ao acúmulo de ausências não justificadas nas sessões deliberações, o deputado teve o mandato cassado por excesso de faltas.

Em novembro do ano passado, o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), acolheu parecer da Secretaria-Geral da Mesa que proíbe parlamentares de registrarem presença e votarem em sessões deliberativas enquanto estiverem fora do território nacional, salvo em caso de missão oficial autorizada pela Casa.

O parecer foi produzido após o deputado federal Alexandre Ramagem (PL-RJ), condenado a 16 anos de prisão por tentativa de golpe , deixar o Brasil em setembro – mês em que a 1ª Turma do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) julgou o núcleo crucial da trama golpista – e participar, de forma remota, da votação do Projeto Antifacção.

“Não há possibilidade regimental de o Deputado Federal registrar presença ou votar por meio do aplicativo Infoleg enquanto estiver fora do território nacional, visto que não se encontra em missão oficial autorizada”, afirma o parecer.

O texto reforça que o exercício do mandato é, por natureza, presencial , conforme o Regimento Interno da Câmara. A participação remota, criada durante a pandemia, permanece restrita a hipóteses específicas.

articles.title: Kilmeade, Hume say Vance ‘not as popular as he thinks he is’ ahead of 2028
articles.summary: Fox News’s Brian Kilmeade and Brit Hume shared their doubts Wednesday about Vice President Vance’s prospects in the 2028 presidential race, questioning whether his close association to President Trump could hurt his chances of winning the Republican nomination. “I just don’t think that Vance is as popular as he thinks he is with Republicans,” Kilmeade…
articles.body:
Fox News’s Brian Kilmeade and Brit Hume shared their doubts Wednesday about Vice President Vance’s prospects in the 2028 presidential race, questioning whether his close association to President Trump could hurt his chances of winning the Republican nomination.

“I just don’t think that Vance is as popular as he thinks he is with Republicans,” Kilmeade said during a conversation with Hume on his radio program “The Brian Kilmeade Show.”

The two were discussing the potential field of presidential contenders in 2028. Hume suggested that Vance, widely viewed as an early front-runner for the GOP nomination, could face challenges depending on how Republicans view Trump by the end of his second term.

“I have a suspicion about Vance, he’s everybody’s ideal front-runner, and he may be,” Hume said, before questioning whether the vice president’s loyalty to Trump would ultimately help or hurt his political ambitions.

“If you’re as attached to the hip to Trump as indeed Vance is, it’s a good question of if that’s a liability or a benefit,” Hume continued. “I think it might end up being a liability.”

Kilmeade disagreed with Hume’s assessment of Trump’s potential influence on the race, arguing that the president’s political standing could improve as his administration advances its agenda.

“I think it’s going to end differently, I actually do,” Kilmeade said, pointing to the administration’s handling of Iran while sharing his skepticism of Vance’s popularity among Republican voters, suggesting the vice president could face a more competitive primary than anticipated.

The conversation also touched on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, another prominent Republican whose name has been floated as a potential 2028 contender.

Hume suggested the GOP primary could attract a crowded field, despite early attention surrounding Vance and Rubio. He also argued that Democrats could face challenges building a campaign around opposition to Trump, who has seen record-low approval ratings in his second term, once the president prepares to leave office.

Trump has not formally endorsed a successor, leaving open questions about whether Vance will enter the 2028 race with the president’s backing or face competition from other members of the administration.

articles.title: Judge declines to block California from counting alleged noncitizen voters’ ballots in DOJ lawsuit
articles.summary: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.
articles.body: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” U.S. District Judge David Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.” What the administration was asking for, he wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.” He also questioned whether the government’s claims of over 20,000 noncitizen voters were accurate. “Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” Carter wrote, pointing to similar allegations the administration had made in a neighboring state. “In Nevada, DHS initially identified up to 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens based on ‘high-confidence’ matches, but later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote. “Had Nevada officials accepted Plaintiff’s allegations there as true, 185 citizens would have been deprived of their vote. This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations.” The Justice Department filed the suit Oct. 15, seeking a court order that the state “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens” and not count them until their citizenship is confirmed. The department said it had compiled “a list of over 20,000 names of people” the government “believes are likely non-citizens.” Attorneys for the state countered that the government’s numbers are unreliable. In a July letter, it put the number of suspect voters at 190,000 and has refused to release information about how it has generated its lists. “Where is the evidence?” an attorney representing California, Christina McCall, said at the hearing Tuesday, calling the government’s allegations “vague” and “not reliable.” Another attorney for the state, Anne Bellows, told the judge “the stakes here are enormous,” arguing the government was trying to force California to initiate an unclear investigation into the citizenship of tens of thousands of people without any clear standards shortly before an election. It “is a recipe for disenfranchisement,” Bellows said. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told Carter: “We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling them what they can’t do.” Essayli said that once the state is made aware of potential noncitizens on its voter rolls, “they need to do something.” “What they cannot do is do nothing and proceed to count the votes,” he said. The judge said that if the government believes there is noncitizen voting, which is a crime, it should bring charges. “Don’t you have the power of indictments?” Carter asked Essayli. “You brought 28 indictments,” he said, referring to a recent announcement by prosecutors of people who have been found to have voted illegally in California in recent years. “You may find others. You have the right to bring that indictment against them.” “You’ve got a remedy, for goodness’ sakes,” Carter said. “Go out and indict.” Essayli on Wednesday bashed the judge’s ruling and said an appeal is underway. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” he said in a statement. “The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit.” The Justice Department has already been to a federal appeals court once in the case. It filed a motion to expedite the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week, after Carter did not act on its request to rule in the matter by Thursday. The appeals court held an emergency hearing Sunday and ruled against the administration 2-1 on Monday. The majority found it did not have jurisdiction because Carter had not yet ruled, but it found the government’s “claimed emergency” was at least partly “a self-constructed one.” “At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’s own delay in filing suit,” Circuit Judge Mark Bennett wrote in the ruling. “The United States has taken issue with California’s voter rolls since at least July 16, when it sent a letter to California’s secretary of state citing its ‘[p]reliminary’ analysis of California’s voter rolls. And neither California’s law permitting the processing of ballots twenty-nine days before an election, nor its law providing for the issuance of mail-in ballots to registered voters, is new,” he wrote. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in a concurring opinion that the government was asking the “court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.” The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote, “We should’ve granted the federal government relief — federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”

images.caption: Election workers sort ballots during early voting in San Francisco on Oct. 21, 2026.

articles.title: DOJ’s California ballot fight rejected by another judge
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s bid to separate 20,000 mail ballots in California that it says are likely noncitizens met another defeat on Wednesday as a trial judge refused to intervene. U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled California can continue to accept the questioned ballots like any other. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s bid to separate 20,000 mail ballots in California that it says are likely noncitizens met another defeat on Wednesday as a trial judge refused to intervene.

U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled California can continue to accept the questioned ballots like any other.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote.

“If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he continued. “Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”

California has raised eyebrows at the veracity of the administration’s list and says it’s not obligated to verify voters’ citizenship in response.

The state has conceded it’s not feasible to segregate a ballot once it’s processed. It would be counted even if later found to be fraudulent. And as Election Day approaches on Tuesday, hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been returned.

It has left the Trump administration pushing for speed, going as far as trying to leapfrog Carter and head straight to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit for a quicker ruling. The appeals court rejected the bid after agreeing to convene on the weekend to hear it.

Carter, an appointee of former President Clinton, has now become the latest judge to reject the effort. He said the administration’s bid would “wreak havoc.”

“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote.

“Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred,” he continued. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”

The Trump administration sued California earlier this month as it alleged that the state was sending 20,000 likely noncitizens ballots for the midterm contests. California has a universal mail-in voting program where all active voters are sent a ballot.

Attorneys for California and Los Angeles County condemn the administration for not sharing who supplied its list. They argue they’re not required to prove voters’ citizenship merely because a sitting administration alleges issues, saying it’s not practical anyways with the current timeline.

“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, wrote on X.

articles.title: Senate Democrats drop $500K in Mississippi
articles.summary: The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) dropped $500,000 in Mississippi’s Senate race supporting Scott Colom (D), who is challenging Trump-backed Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). The new ad focused on Colom’s record as a district attorney in the Magnolia State as the Democrat stated he’ll “take on anyone who stands in the way of what’s best…
articles.body:
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) dropped $500,000 in Mississippi’s Senate race supporting Scott Colom (D), who is challenging Trump-backed Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.).

The new ad focused on Colom’s record as a district attorney in the Magnolia State as the Democrat stated he’ll “take on anyone who stands in the way of what’s best for Mississippi,” while alleging Hyde-Smith had “forgotten us.”

“Senate Democrats have expanded the battleground deep into Republican territory and we are continuing to pursue every path possible to win a Senate majority,” a spokesperson for the DSCC, Tommy Garcia, said in a statement .

The ad marked the first time the DSCC has poured money into this race, adding Mississippi to its list of targets as the party seeks to regain control of the upper chamber.

The Senate Majority PAC (SMP), a top Democratic super PAC, already launched a $1.2 million ad campaign for Colom. The competitiveness of the race has drawn the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund to spend more than $1 million in an effort to defend Hyde-Smith’s seat.

Democrats face an uphill battle as the last time Mississippi a Democratic senator statewide was in 1982 and President Trump carried it by 23 percentage points in 2024.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, shifted the Mississippi Senate race from solid Republican to lean Republican — another sign that Republicans may have a tougher fight than usual to hold the seat.

Trump headlined a rally in Mississippi which the GOP are hoping will increase turnout in an election cycle where the party is on the defensive.

Mississippi-based Republican strategist Hayes Dent told The Hill earlier this week that there are high levels of frustration among Republicans against Trump.

“When you go and tell everybody you’re going to get us out of wars, you’re going to drain the swamp, you’re going to cut gas prices, you’re going to do all of this, and none of that is occurring, people get frustrated,” Dent said.

Meanwhile, Colom has the backing of former President Obama who cut a 30-second ad spot for him. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) have all also made stops in Mississippi this month.

articles.title: Trump calls alleged Alaska Senate spoiler scheme ‘voter fraud at the highest level’
articles.summary: President Trump criticized Senate Democrats and former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign on Wednesday amid allegations that the two worked together to put a spoiler candidate on the ballot in an effort to boost their party in the Alaska Senate race. “This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump said while rallying in Chillicothe,…
articles.body:
President Trump criticized Senate Democrats and former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign on Wednesday amid allegations that the two worked together to put a spoiler candidate on the ballot in an effort to boost their party in the Alaska Senate race.

“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump said while rallying in Chillicothe, Ohio, for GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted, both of whom are locked in tight battles next Tuesday.

“That’s what they’re good at – cheating,” the president added.

The New York Times reported earlier on Wednesday that operatives of Peltola’s campaign and the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were allegedly involved in recruiting spoiler candidates to the Alaska Senate race, including the “undeclared” candidate Dan J. Sullivan appearing on the Senate ballot, as a way to siphon votes away from the GOP incumbent.

Both Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) issued statements saying they had no involvement in such a scheme.

“Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight,” a Peltola campaign spokesperson told The Hill in a statement. “The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”

The DSCC also separately said in a statement they had “no involvement” in the spoiler Sullivan effort.

Recruiting spoiler candidates is not a new phenomenon as it’s a tactic that’s been legally used by both parties in the state before.

However, Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who’s been support of Peltola in the past, criticized Democrats for allegedly meddling in the Alaska Senate race – particularly as they’ve made threats to democracy a core message of theirs against the GOP.

Trump earlier on Wednesday called for both Peltola and the spoiler candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.

articles.title: Obama knocks White House’s response to Cheesecake Factory jab: ‘These are not serious people’
articles.summary: Former President Obama on Wednesday responded to uproar over a recent campaign trail jab at President Trump’s White House decorations, slamming Republicans for focusing more on the joke than on the economy. “They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke,” Obama said during a campaign rally in Georgia.…
articles.body:
Former President Obama on Wednesday responded to uproar over a recent campaign trail jab at President Trump’s White House decorations, slamming Republicans for focusing more on the joke than on the economy.

“They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke,” Obama said during a campaign rally in Georgia. “This is what I mean when I say these are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”

Obama had quipped during a recent campaign stop in Cleveland, Ohio, that Trump’s taste in renovations worth a reported $900 million has the White House “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, it’s just gold everywhere,” referring to the Iraqi palaces that were famously adorned with gold decor.

Trump hit back from the road as he makes his own midterm travel blitz, touting the restaurant chain as a “very successful company” and calling Obama “a lousy president.”

“It’s not about money. It’s about seeing. Guys like Obama don’t see it. He doesn’t see dirt, he doesn’t see filth, he doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building,” Trump said. “For you to say it was a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”

Trump has spearheaded a pricey overhaul to the Rose Garden and constructed a new granite helipad on the South Lawn, in addition to updating decor and adding signage in the gold color he’s favored since his first administration.

Rallying for Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia on Wednesday, Obama shrugged off the outcry, saying he’d “heard the president was not happy” with his campaign-trail roast.

“First of all, let me get this on the record. I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory? I lived at Chuck E. Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and the Cheesecake Factory. That was my jam for about a decade,” Obama said.

“Of course, the real problem is the price has gotten so high, a lot of folks can barely afford to go out to eat, so you would think that this administration would be spending time worrying about that. But that was the interesting thing about how the administration responded to the speech I gave.”

Obama argued that the administration “did not dispute” his argument that they were directly responsible for rising prices, a major midterm issue for voters across the country, and expressing shock that the president “wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison.”

He pointed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who mocked the former president outside of a Cheesecake Factory in Washington after the comments, saying he “never thought of” having his own Treasury Secretary, Tim Geithner, make a similar move.

As he railed against Republicans in Congress for not holding Trump to account on the economy and more, Obama also made reference to furor over a tan suit he wore as he spoke about foreign issues during his second presidential term.

“I am old enough to remember when a president wearing a tan suit was a major national controversy,” the former president quipped. “They were very upset, and I know I looked good in that suit.”

The Cheesecake Factory spat comes in the closing days of a highly competitive election cycle that’s brought both Trump and Obama out to stump for candidates in key races.

Obama’s appearance in the Peach State sought to rally voters for Ossoff, “not because he looks like a Kennedy or handsome in the videos” but because he can “stir up some good trouble,” the president said — along with Lance Bottoms, who he described as “in it for the right reasons.”

The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), gives Ossoff an 89 percent chance of beating his GOP opponent, Rep. Mike Collins, to win a second term in the Senate.

The governor’s race is tighter, with Bottoms only narrowly favored in a toss-up race against Republican billionaire Rick Jackson to replace term-limited Gov. Brian Kemp (R).

images.caption: Former President Barack Obama speaks in support of Democratic candidates Sen. Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, Morrow, Ga. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)

articles.title: El-Sayed responds to Stevens’s fiancée endorsing Rogers
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed responded to his former primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) fiancée endorsing his GOP opponent former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). “Well, I’m building a movement to take on the challenges that Donald Trump is facing. If folks have issues that are more important to them than that, that’s fine,” El-Sayed…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed responded to his former primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) fiancée endorsing his GOP opponent former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

“Well, I’m building a movement to take on the challenges that Donald Trump is facing. If folks have issues that are more important to them than that, that’s fine,” El-Sayed said while at a campaign event Wednesday. “That’s their choice. But to me, this election is about control of the United States Senate.”

He continued that this election was about “putting a check on” President Trump and “addressing his effort to try and take away everything from religious freedom to our voting rights to union rights to healthcare.”

“I’m welcoming a big tent of folks to come together around the effort to push back on Trump,” El-Sayed continued. “And I hope that as many folks out there can join. You know, we’ve felt really strong about our ability to bring people together. There are always going to be some folks who have different opinions, and they’re welcome to that. That’s the beauty of democracy.”

In an interview with The Detroit News on Wednesday, Stevens’s fiancée, Jason Turkish, accused the Democrat of using antisemitic language. He added that “we have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul.”

The pair announced their engagement in August following El-Sayed’s victory over Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. Stevens publicly backed El-Sayed after this loss, but she has not campaigned alongside him in several months. She also sidestepped questions earlier this week concerning her support for El-Sayed.

“Look, I’m on the Democratic ticket. You know, I can’t say that I agree with everything that’s gone on,” she said on CNN . “I wish that first debate had been more about you know that rubber stamp for Trump because we got a lot of chaos in Michigan.”

The Cook Political Report rated the race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) a “toss up.” Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner, favored El-Sayed over Rogers, giving the Democrat a 69 percent of winning compared to the Republican’s 31 percent odds.

articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) criticized rapper Nicki Minaj on Wednesday, saying President Trump’s rallies were “poisoning” the artist’s mind.

“Maybe she oughta get outside and get offline a little more,” Hochul told reporters . “And stop going to Trump rallies, it’s kinda poisoning your mind.”

The Empire State governor was responding to a post by Minaj from Wednesday afternoon where she called Hochul an “evil woman.”

“The Democratic Party should forfeit her seat because even if she wins, she will be of great consequence to them,” Minaj – who called herself Trump’s “ No. 1 fan ” – wrote on social platform X .

“Downward spiral for her. She will not escape God’s wrath. She did not denounce evil when she had the chance,” she concluded.

In 2020, Minaj said she would not “jump on the Donald Trump bandwagon,” but in recent years she’s become a vocal supporter of the president and the GOP. Speaking at a recent Michigan campaign rally, Minaj pledged her support for Trump, saying, “if you run again, I will support you again.”

She has also been floated as a possible replacement for former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia by White House communications director Steven Cheung. It’s unclear how serious Cheung is about hiring Minaj as one of the administration’s top officials.

During her various appearances with administration officials, Minaj has echoed Trump’s false claims regarding the 2020 election, backed the president after he claimed that Christians in Nigeria were persecuted and promoted the debut of Trump accounts .

Hochul’s gubernatorial opponent Bruce Blakeman (R) also chimed in , telling Minaj on social media, “Nicki, I’ve got the U-Haul ready. It’s time to fire the worst governor in America.”

Blakeman is currently trailing Hochul, according to recent Siena University polling . The poll found Hochul now manages a 14-point lead compared to leading Blakeman by 9-points in September.

Siena University noted that 68 percent of respondents believed Hochul would win the election. Forty percent of Republican respondents expressed they believed the New York governor would win reelection.

articles.title: Hegseth fires the Pentagon's top military planner even as Trump considers new Iran strikes
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war.

Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October.

The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic.

A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said "the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation" and they "wish him and his family the best."

Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran.

Trump has vowed to "finish the job" in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week.

U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes.

A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region .

Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5.

He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday.

Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions.

"I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30.

Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."

Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report.

articles.title: Judge rejects Trump effort to block California ‘noncitizen’ ballots
articles.summary: More than 100 subpoenas issued across 13 states as government ramps up search for alleged noncitizen voters.
articles.body:
A United States judge has rejected a Department of Justice request to temporarily halt California from counting mail ballots from a list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens just six days before the country’s midterm elections.

US District Judge David Carter’s ruling on Wednesday came as US President Donald Trump expands efforts to search for alleged noncitizen voters, with subpoenas issued in at least 13 states.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote on Wednesday.

The judge, a 1998 appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department’s last-minute request to exclude more than 20,000 ballots ran afoul of “longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections”.

The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals and did not immediately respond to requests for comment by the Reuters news agency.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on October 15, a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before Tuesday’s election, when voters will choose which party controls Congress as well as their state and local representatives.

The decision marks the latest setback in Trump’s effort to expand the federal government’s role in elections ahead of the legislative midterms, as his Republican Party fights to retain control of both houses of Congress.

The Trump administration issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states , both Republican- and Democratic-leaning.

Most of the subpoenas Reuters documented were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known.

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest close midterm results, despite scant evidence that noncitizen voting is widespread.

Also on Wednesday, Democracy Docket, a US media platform that tracks election litigation, reported that the Department of Justice list of alleged noncitizen voters “appears to have been created using a deeply flawed process” that could disenfranchise US citizen voters beyond California.

In a court filing, a government whistleblower revealed that voters were being scrutinised nationwide, not just in California, as part of the federal government’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative” investigation, the group reported. The whistleblower warned that “the current process is knowingly sweeping known US citizens in as potentially ‘unlawful voters'”.

California has said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data” and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters. Democracy Docket reported that in Los Angeles County, one in four voters on the “noncitizen” list were born in the US.
